Mr. Speaker, members of the house will have read with regret the announcement that His Majesty Tuanku Abdul Rahman, the paramount ruler of Malaya, died this morning in Kuala Lumpur. His Majesty had been Malaya's distinguished head of state since that country became independent in 1957. He had played a significant part in fostering Malaya's links with the commonwealth, and in his capacity as head of state in a parliamentary democracy he had been closely associated with Malaya's admirable record of economic and political progress.
I shall always remember the generous hospitality extended to me on the occasion of my visit there, at which time he spoke in most glowing terms of Canada and its relationship with his country. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, March 18, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr.	Fleming	(Eglinton)-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to provide certain alternative arrangements for payment, either by Canada through the Canadian Universities Foundation or directly by a province, of the grants to institutions of higher learning presently paid under the authority of the Appropriation Act: and also to extend for a further period of two years the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the
Dominion-Provincial Relations purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
(Translation):

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the
debate was adjourned the other day, I was recalling certain remarks made last year by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) in justification of his stand on federal grants to universities. In his view, the exclusive rights of the provinces in the field of education, under section 93 of the act of 1867, did not apply to institutions of higher learning, and his suggestion, one of great import, was summed up as follows:
Therefore, I repeat that, in my opinion, the fathers of confederation, acting in good faith, have given no consideration whatever to universities, when the provision on education was inserted in section 93.
Without going that far, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said on July 18 last something that amounted to about the same thing, as reported on page 6374 of Hansard of that date. I quote:
Since they were established in 1951 we have always said that such grants-
The federal grants to universities.
-were constitutional.
And as if to convince himself further, the hon. member went on to say:
This system of grants was established as a direct compensation to Canadian universities for the national and international role that they are called upon to play and which greatly benefits the nation as a whole and the federal government itself.
Three days later, that statement of the hon. member for Laurier prompted Mr. Gerard Filion, manager of Le Devoir, to make the following comments:
Need we again point out that the Liberal theory put forward by Mr. Chevrier is basically unacceptable. According to the hon. member for Laurier, university grants are justified by the national and international character of those institutions of higher learning. It will be noted that the former minister fails to base his arguments on legal grounds-
This is still Mr. Filion speaking.
-because the texts are perfectly clear. Only the provinces have the right to legislate in educational matters, which implies that they have an exclusive right to collect funds for the maintenance of schools.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the hon. members for Laurier and Megantic would have had quite a bit of trouble finding some legal basis for their statements. To suggest, as did the hon. member for Megantic, that the fathers of confederation never had universities or higher education in mind, when they conferred upon the provinces exclusive powers in the educational field, is to have a very poor opinion of the knowledge and foresight of the Macdonalds, Cartiers and
2810	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations others. What is more, this is an historical error which should be refuted if to prevent the serious consequences to which it might again expose us.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, contrary to what the hon. member for Megantic seems to think, Laval was not the only Quebec university in 1867. There were also Bishop and McGill colleges. Furthermore, there were already some classical colleges where, in half the courses, university training in the Anglo-Saxon sense of the word, was being provided.
In fact, if we refer to the French edition of the Journal of Public Education, for that date, we see that, as early as March 1857, there were in United Canada five universities, two of them in Upper Canada and thirty three colleges, twenty five of them in Lower Canada.
If, at the time of confederation, Laval University was not yet getting any help from the government, the situation was different with regard to McGill and Bishop colleges, and I would refer the hon. member to the Journal of Education, English version, of 1864, volume 80, pages 157 and 158. Moreover, he will find there a list of eleven colleges that were already receiving grants. I fail to see how the politicians of 1867 were unaware of those facts.
Besides, the grants were being drawn out of specific funds and distributed under existing laws. In fact, if we refer to the revised statutes of Lower Canada, 1860, chapter 15, Part 3, we find there an "act concerning a provincial allowance in favour of higher education-and normal and common schools". It establishes an investment fund made up mostly of assets confiscated from the Jesuits. The superintendent of education for Lower Canada, in conjunction with the governor in council, is entrusted with the distribution of the returns. I quote section 6:
-for and between such universities, colleges, seminaries, academies, lycees or high schools, model schools and educational institutions, other than ordinary elementary schools.
On the other hand, in chapter XVII of the same statutes, there is the act concerning the Royal Institute for the Advancement of Science. According to that act, which incidentally, is but the outcome of several laws enacted over nearly a quarter of a century, the trustees are incorporated and their corporation holds in trust all lands and property donated by the founder of McGill college and by other benefactors, to help that institution carry on its mission.
How can we imagine that our legislators, in 1867, were unaware of those laws? Quite the contrary, they knew them so well that, in


Appendix 4 of the act of 1867, they had considered as an "asset becoming the common property of Ontario and Quebec", among other things:
-the capital assets of universities-
And also:
-the Royal Institute.
Is that not clear and precise enough?
And there is more.	When the federal
statutes were revised in 1887, the commissioners who were setting out the matters over which the respective powers had jurisdiction pointed out very clearly that both the above-mentioned laws should be embodied in the revised statutes of Lower Canada.
In the light of those facts and laws, I am surely justified in coming to the conclusion that not only did our public men, in 1867, have both universities and classical colleges in mind when they sought and obtained from the imperial parliament that the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over education, but in transferring to them the public funds, which, at the time, served to provide in part for those schools of higher learning, they clearly indicated their wish to let the provinces subsidize those schools. And this will, far from being merely a whim, fulfilled the essential conditions laid down by Lower Canada for joining the confederation. I turn to the testimony of George Brown himself who stated:
(Text):
Education, the rights of property and the civil law, we were compelled to leave to the local governments, in order to afford that protection which the lower Canadians claim for their language and their laws and their peculiar institutions.
(Translation):
Reference: Edward Whelan, The Union of the British provinces, 1865, page 187.
If we assume that federal participation in the financing of universities had really been in accord with the constitution, how can we imagine that none of our government leaders for more than 80 years, had not an inkling of it being so. Have they been remiss in their obligations towards institutions of higher learning, or were they simply poor ignoramuses? Because, let us not forget it, it is only through the Massey commission report, published on June 1, 1951, that the great discovery was made on the basis of which it was recommended:
-that the federal government make annual contributions to support the work of the universities on the basis of the population of each of the provinces of Canada.
And it was in that same month, June of that year, that was passed as the first contribution of the kind since confederation.

Once the precedent had been set-and Heaven knows the power of precedent under British law-it seemed only natural to repeat it in 1952, especially as the Massey report recommendation explicitly mentioned the word "annual". However, in that particular instance, important amendments were made to the terms of item No. 699, which then remained unchanged until 1956.
First, under the 1952 legislation, institutions qualifying for grants had to be recognized both by the federal government and by the provincial government in the province where they were operating. Moreover- and this is even more serious-the federal Minister of Finance was given the responsibility of defining the expressions "university level" and "university degree". And to give practical application to this utterly fantastic power, the government, on January 9, 1952, passed order in council P.C. 123, which gave a federal definition of those terms, and also of the terms "student" and "university". Just as a sample, let me quote the definition given of the phrase "university level":
With regard to a province, a more advanced curriculum than is generally accepted in the provinces as a prerequisite to university enrolment.
That, you must admit, was a dangerous definition, the terms being so vague and indefinite.
Far from improving the situation, those conditions and terms only made it worse. In the province of Quebec, in particular, where universities and affiliated classical colleges control their own curricula and enjoy the greatest degree of freedom, a freedom that enables them to maintain the peculiar character of our educational system which is so well adapted to the cultural traditions of our people, how could such an intrusion be accepted in a field which the province regards with such pride and jealousy? That time, no further compromise was possible, and federal grants were spectacularly rejected. *
There was another and quite serious danger. In a country like ours, where two living cultures are found beside each other, where programs and methods of education are based on either of them according to the ethnical element for which they are meant, where the structures of our institutions of higher learning differ among themselves as much as Quebec differs from the other provinces, it was extremely dangerous to give to each of the four designations "student", "university", "university level" and "university degree" a single definition applying to the whole country. Thus, according to a remark made by the Rev. Father Vanier, who was rector of Jean-de-Brebeuf
Dominion-Provincial Relations college, "the heart and soul of the Anglo-Saxon type of universities is the "college", especially the faculty of arts and sciences where the student registers after the four or five years high school course, whereas, generally speaking, in Quebec, the B.A. degree which opens the door to the great faculties, is awarded only to students who have followed courses in letters, philosophy and applied sciences during four additional years at college.
Both those methods give excellent results; but I point out those facts only to show one of the basic differences between them, differences that the legislator had to take into consideration.
Is it surprising, after that-and it is the same educator who recalled it in December 1956-that newspapers from Halifax to Vancouver charged those who were responsible for this policy of federal grants to universities with the secret desire of achieving cultural unification and with endeavouring to put an end to the particularism of the province of Quebec.
The Minister of Finance will have had the merit of recognizing the full implications of the extremely serious objections we had made to the policy adopted by the federal government in 1951. Rejecting certain suggestions made by the hon. member for Laurier, he expressed his views on July 19 of last year, in these words:
The province of Quebec has a point of view in regard to education which I think all hon. members of this committee have a duty to recognize. It is patent that a different view altogether is taken of this subject in the province of Quebec from the view that is taken in the other provinces of Canada.
I am still quoting from the minister's statement:
Those who know the history of the province of Quebec understand the point of view of that province today and will know that Quebec regards this exclusive jurisdiction over education as something fundamental to the ethnic survival of that province and its people. This has been the view of the people of Quebec down through the years, that its jurisdiction over education is the sheet anchor of the survival of the culture, the language and the institutions of the province.
The minister added:
I also say to the members of this committee that at this time no modification can be introduced into this item since the item has been known to universities which are free to accept their share and they are counting on it.
And the Minister of Finance went on to say:
But, Mr. Chairman, having regard to the fact that nearly all of the universities of one province of this country are not receiving their share of these grants, before such an item or any item on this subject is presented to the house in another

Dominion-Provincial Relations year a most intensive effort must be made to grapple with this very great difficulty. For my part, X give the committee my personal assurance that anything I can do to help to resolve this difficulty will certainly be done if effort and understanding can do it.
Those comments and this solemn pledge fully answered the wish that some of us Conservative members of the province of Quebec, had felt bound to express clearly and frankly. For my part, dealing with this problem in the house on April 22, 1959, I pointed out among other things-I apologize for quoting from my own speech-the following:
Whatever may be the value and strength of the precedent, in a federated country such as ours, the rights and powers conferred by the constitution are not subject to prescription. They never lapse. And this tenet is all the more to the point since the province of Quebec has never failed to abide by section 93 in its entirety. Therefore its position is absolutely unassailable and every effort of this government, in co-operation with the government of Quebec, should aim at finding as soon as possible a way to settle this thorny problem and to make it easier for the province to exercise its powers most freely in this field.
Then, after putting forward a few suggestions, I concluded with the following words:
I repeat, Mr. Speaker-and X close my remarks with that statement-that, faced with the importance of that problem of federal grants to university teaching; faced with the conflicts of opinions which they arouse in the province of Quebec; faced with the resistance shown by the Quebec government, in order to fully retain the exercise of a right all its own; faced with the deep-seated reasons motivating its attachment to that right, its will to defend and maintain it, I do hope the problem will be on the agenda of the next federal-provincial conference; that it will be approached and discussed with frankness and in a spirit of co-operation and, above all, I do hope it will be solved through some agreement. That will take into account the very basis of federalism, which may be summed up in two words; unity in diversity.
Since then, there have been talks between the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada and the hon. Minister of Finance, and the three premiers who, over a very short period of time, have successively headed the province of Quebec. This resolution is, in a way, the outcome of the courageous efforts made on both sides. Although, in principle, it remains based on the precedent of 1951 which, since then, has recurred each year, it might open the way to provinces that will see fit to use the taxation rights to which they are entitled and which they need to subsidize higher learning. It indicates, in the minds of our leaders, a tendency that Mr. Andre Laurendeau in he Devoir of December 30, 1959-

It indicates, in the minds of our leaders, a tendency that Mr. Andre Laurendeau, in he Devoir of December 30, 1959, described as definite, sound and shrewd. maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Of course, you may.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I shall ask it in English and the hon. member may reply in French.
(Text):
I understood the hon. gentleman to quote with approval a citation to the effect that the provincial government of Quebec had been giving assistance to institutions of higher learning outside the province of Quebec. Am I correct in thinking that the hon. gentleman did quote such a citation with approval? I refer to the University of Ottawa, for example. Do I understand that the hon. gentleman approves of that conduct?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I should like to reply in English but I may not be able to do it too distinctly, and I shall therefore reply in French.
(Translation):
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is true that the province of Quebec has on occasion contributed funds to the University of Ottawa, and also, I think, to certain universities in Nova Scotia. I must say however that

they were donations voted by the provincial legislature, and whether it was on an annual basis, I cannot say. They are donations voted by the Quebec legislature to help other French groups, or rather universities attended by French-speaking students.
As far as I know it is on that basis that such donations are sometimes voted for the benefit of those educational institutions of French culture.
(Text):

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a second question? Will the hon. gentleman explain to me what is the difference in principle between the government of Quebec voting money to institutions outside that province, which are under the jurisdiction of another province, and the parliament of Canada voting money to free institutions in this free country of Canada, say for example those of the English language in the province of Quebec, with no strings attached; voted annually, as they were in this parliament? Can the hon. gentleman explain to me any difference in principle there?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Yes. The difference is in the constitution: the difference is in section 93. By section 93 this power is given to the provinces; it is not given to the federal government.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think the government of Quebec has any right to be giving money to a university in Ontario, and thereby, according to him, to interfere with the educational autonomy of the province of Ontario?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It is quite different. First of all, the right is inscribed in section 93 without any reservation at all. Second, the province of Quebec has a role to play in Canada because there is a French ethnic group in the country, and the province of Quebec has cultural obligations not only in the province but in all Canada.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: In all Canada; and that is why the province of Quebec by his government voted certain grants to universities outside of Quebec, at the request of those universities and with the implied consent of the governments of those provinces. (Translation):

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Before going into my remarks, let me first read the resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act to provide certain alternative arrangements for payment, either by Canada through the Canadian Universities Foundation or directly by a province, of the grants to institutions of higher learning presently paid under the authority of the Appropriation Act: and also to extend for a further period of two years the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
There are therefore two parts to this resolution. The first deals with arrangements between the federal government and the provinces with regard to grants to universities.
All hon. members know that in the province of Quebec the universities since 1951-52 have been forced by the government, and particularly by the former premier of Quebec, the Hon. Maurice Duplessis, to refuse the grants offered to them by the federal government.
As I say, universities had been forced by the former premier of the province of Quebec, because he told them openly: Leaders of universities and classical colleges must choose between grants from Ottawa and grants from Quebec.

After receiving an amount of $2,225,800 for the year 1951-52, the universities accepted federal grants that year only and then were deprived of them because of the stand taken by the former Quebec premier, Hon. Mr. Duplessis.
The universities will now be getting federal grants, especially those that have been paid since 1956, because the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, was wise enough

However, Mr. Chairman, allow me to say that I am fully in favour of grants to all universities and classical colleges of Canada.
It is very easy to understand the reasons why the federal government has instituted those grants. It has instituted them at the request of the majority of the provinces. As all hon. members know, in some provinces universities give technical and professional training to their citizens, and when the latter graduate instead of remaining in their own province to give it the benefit of their knowledge they have to go, in many cases, into another province to find work, so that it is the other provinces which benefit from the amounts paid by the citizens of one province to train part of the population. It is only fair that, in return, the federal government should redistribute certain grants to the universities and classical colleges of Canada.

As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, the province of Quebec lost considerable amounts for educational purposes, and I feel sure that in accepting the new formula, Quebec universities and classical colleges will be getting something to which they are entitled, because from the letter or letters, or the exchange of letters, between the former premier of the province of Quebec, the hon. Mr. Paul Sauve, and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker), it is my understanding that only the tax collector is changed, and nothing else.
At the present time, Ottawa collects the taxes and redistributes them to universities on the basis of $1.50 per capita in each province. Under the new formula, no longer will Ottawa be collecting those funds and distributing them to the various universities. That will be done by the province or provinces. So far, however, only the province of Quebec has expressed the desire to collect this 1 per cent tax on corporations. An interesting point is that, according to the correspondence, the province of Quebec will not be allowed to keep this 1 per cent; it will only be allowed to keep the equivalent of $1.50 multiplied by its population. The balance will be handed over to Ottawa, which will keep it.
The position has changed. Now the province of Quebec will collect the tax instead of Ottawa.
I have nothing more to add to my remarks. I shall wait to study the bill, and I shall probably have further comments to make at that time.

Mr. Chairman, if we refer to Hansard of Saturday, July 18, 1959, when university grants were being discussed, we note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) replied as follows to the hon. member for Laurier:
Every university that I know of in Canada is subject to provincial jurisdiction. There is no such thing as a university created by federal authority, and the same applies to municipalities.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is made quite clear that these were referred to as provincial institutions, and I think hon. members will conclude that the hon. member for Laurier was drawing a very long bow when he suggested that this
2818	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations reference to universities as provincial institutions connoted some thought of making federal contributions to the cost of primary and secondary education. Nothing could be further from the truth. Nothing could be further from the intention of the government.
This quotation from the Minister of Finance may be found on page 6391 of Hansard for July 18, 1959.
The hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) was rather critical a moment ago, and he made a comparison which, in my opinion, was not proper when he referred to gifts made by the Quebec government to certain educational institutions in other provinces. I would point out to him that education is under provincial jurisdiction and that even if the province of Quebec made a gift to the Ottawa university I do not believe that in so doing it interfered with the rights of the Ontario government in that field.
Besides, a grant always has certain conditions attached to it. A grant has always strings attached to it, whereas a gift is unconditional. A gift may be refused or accepted. A grant has always conditions attached to it.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance who, in co-operation with the Quebec premier, has worked out an agreement on this problem.
We cannot forget the sincere attitude adopted by Quebec premiers who have taken part in those negotiations for many years. Mr. Duplessis has stoutly defended the rights of an autonomist province within a great confederation. Mr. Duplessis, in my opinion, was actually voicing the opinion of his province, the province of Quebec, in basing himself on the constitution. Everybody knows, besides, that the Tremblay report agrees with the attitude taken by the premier of Quebec at the time. The educational institutions, the elite, in a word the whole province of Quebec, have supported the late Hon. Maurice Duplessis who, for a while, was the only one in the country to defend the autonomy of the province of Quebec, and thus of all the other provinces. In fact, several premiers said later that Maurice Duplessis was right, that the federal government was going too far in too many fields which do not concern it.
Need I call to witness a Liberal from Newfoundland who thoroughly agrees with the stand the late Hon. Mr. Duplessis had taken. In fact Le Devoir of July 20, 1959 said:
Liberal senator Wishart Robertson, just before the adoption by the Senate Saturday of the act concerning the grants to Newfoundland, said that the


federal-provincial tax-sharing agreements were ridiculous and nonsensical. "We have given rise," he said, "to an absurd situation where a government collects money to give it to other governments-* This system has made suppliants of at least eight of the ten provincial governments-It results in unending controversies which, in my opinion, will only become worse in the immediate future. The attitude of Premier Duplessis towards this ridiculous problem is more logical than that of the other federal and provincial negotiators", the senator added. He simplifies the problem in these words: "Give up a field to us and we will collect our own taxes and we will pay our own expenditures."
Mr. Chairman, Hon. Maurice Duplessis not only expressed the point of view, as I said earlier, of the province of Quebec, but also that of all the provinces, because he wanted to safeguard the confederation pact. Besides, he had the support of the people of Quebec.
His successor endeavoured to find a middle term to bring about an agreement. Unfortunately, death came to him suddenly. Thus, it became the responsibility of the present premier of Quebec, whom I have the honour to have among my loyal constituents, to bring a true solution to this crucial problem.
Mr. Chairman, the agreement between the federal government and the province of Quebec will be an example. This gesture will not only consolidate national unity, but will contribute to the formation of a truly Canadian mentality.
The problem of the relations between the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures is as old as confederation itself. We can even say that the problem existed before, since as early as the Charlottetown meeting in 1864, it became quite clear that the apportionment of powers within the framework of a federal state would not be achieved without certain clashes and incidents.
It is not our purpose to attempt today to solve that problem or even to find a cure-all formula for all the evils resulting from the co-existence of a federal state and ten provincial governments.
The British North America Act is a document bearing the stamp of wisdom resulting from the long experience which initiators acquired through their contacts with the Canadian people in the administration of public affairs. The fathers of confederation devoted many years to draft a final text which was to combine with its nature of a pact between the contracting parties the legislative character resulting from its promulgation as an imperial statute. The fathers of confederation did

not delude themselves as to the difficulty of the problems which were arising and which would arise between the federal authority and the provincial entities.
Therefore it was clearly stated in section 93 of the British North America Act what would be the respective powers of the central government and of the provinces. However, nothing is final in this world, not even a British law, and that is why since 1867 many commissions have been established to study certain aspects of the relations between the federal authority and the provinces. Those of us who have had the opportunity and the patience to read the voluminous report of the Rowell-Sirois commission which report, incidentally, was centralistic, or the reports of the various federal-provincial conferences were amazed, not to say dumbfounded, at the complexity of the problems and especially of the differences of opinions put forward by the various parties concerned. It is no use deluding ourselves; there is something wrong between the federal government and the provinces. Speeches and briefs dealing with that problem clearly indicate two different stands, perhaps not irreconcilable, but certainly diametrically opposed. The federal government and the provinces do not speak the same language and that is the cause of the increasing difficulties.
Under the terms of the constitution itself, Ottawa has certain clearly defined powers while the provinces have others also well spelled out. But besides that the federal government has what we call the residual powers, which means that all that is not specifically provincial is automatically federal, and even as members of this house, we are not at all convinced that this solution is a very appropriate one. The federal government is jealous of its prerogatives and rightly so. We would be the first to rise as one to defend the rights of federal government against any threat from within or from without. We do not want foreign countries to tell us how to administer our country, just as we have no intention to be dictated to by the provinces.
On the other hand, if we have those rights, the provinces also have theirs, and it would be ungracious not to recognize it. No province is thinking of encroaching on the federal field, and we fail to see why the Ottawa government would be presumptuous to the point of wanting to substitute itself to the provincial authorities in the fields vested in them.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
I would point out, as an example, that under the constitution of Canada, indirect taxation and certain rights in the field of direct taxation come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government. The same constitution imposes specific and important obligations on the provinces, wherefrom it ensues that the same provinces have a right to collect a revenue from direct taxes. This is true to such a degree that for more that half a century there was no question about the collection of direct taxes. And even when federal income tax was established, the federal minister of finance stated that it was only a temporary measure to be considered as a wartime measure. It was in this same House of Commons that Sir Thomas White stated in 1917:
Income tax comes especially within provincial jurisdiction; this tax particularly meets the purposes of the province and of municipalities.
The same applies to estates, because until 1942 the federal government had stayed away from that taxation field, since it is closely related to civil rights and property. Those two infringements of the rights vested in the provinces are both equally unbearable. There is no need to be a learned economist to understand that what is provincial belongs to the provinces and what is federal comes under the central or centralizing government. We are always under the impression that only the province of Quebec asks for the restitution of the funds stolen from the provinces by the federal government. There is also an attempt to suggest that the formula of the return to the provinces of their own rights and funds was conceived by the former Quebec premier, the late Hon. Mr. Duplessis. Yet, who stated this in 1867:
Lower Canada is rightly proud of its ancestral customs and traditions; it is bound by its particular institutions and it will only enter into confederation with the assurance of retaining them.
It was Lord Carnarvon.
To quote another testimony, which is not precisely from a member of the present Quebec cabinet, may I repeat that:
The existence of the provinces preceded that of the Dominion of Canada, and it is from them that it got its powers. The provinces are sovereign within the limits of their attributes and any attack against that sovereignty is a violation of the federal pact.
And who, Mr. Chairman, made such a judicious comment? None other than a great premier of Canada's oldest province, the Hon. Honore Mercier, in 1884. I think no

Dominion-Provincial Relations one could accuse him of being a bad Canadian or a poor Liberal.
That is the position. From a constitutional point of view, the rights are clearly-defined. The federal government has its own, and provincial legislatures also have theirs. There can be no question, for emergency or other reasons, to change this arrangement without first obtaining the consent of all parties to confederation. That is the law of the land. If it is bad, then it can always be changed, but in the meantime, it should be enforced, without any haggling or discrimination.
Once it is admitted that the claims of the provinces are justified-and I say provinces purposely, because it is not only Quebec- there remains the problem of finding a solution to this anomaly. From a practical point of view, such a situation cannot last indefinitely. It has lasted for too many years already. Let us face the facts as shown to us by history. It is a government which, for national emergency reasons, decided to invade the field of provincial revenues, at the time the great war was in its most sinister period. We do not want to criticize our predecessors for it, because they did what the circumstances forced them to do at the time. But it belongs to another great government, that of the Right Hon. Mr. Diefen-baker, to correct that anomaly. Thus, the names of Borden and Diefenbaker once again will be united in history, because the former saved Canada from the German threat, and the latter will have saved national unity. It is not a matter of a favour asked by the province of Quebec; it is a matter of justice for all provinces; we are not asking for charity, but for equity.
It must, in fact, be recognized that citizens, and this is the price which we must pay for belonging to a federal state, have a dual responsibility as citizens, not to say a dual citizenship, or a dual allegiance. Indeed they are, for certain things, under the federal government and for others under a provincial administration. But such dual citizenship also implies a dual responsibility. In order to satisfy it, it is essential that Canadians have access to the legal financial means put at their disposal by the constitution.
The fathers of confederation wanted to endow every Canadian with the means of discharging his responsibility as a good citizen and also with the facilities needed for this purpose. It is therefore not up to us to re-

vise that position today, and even if an injustice has been done in the past, we must strive to repair the wrong that has been done.
It is utterly futile, not to say immoral, to maintain that one authority will levy taxes and hand them over in some form or other to the other power which forms the confed-erative association. Those who hold the purse strings can spend and control. Indeed, from 1887 on, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was born at St. Lin, in the Laurentians, in the riding of l'Assomption which I have the honour to represent in this house, said:
The principle whereby a government levies revenues for another to spend is basically wrong.
Is there any need to repeat, in this respect, the views of a Canadian whom our opponents hardly would call anti-Liberal. Indeed, it was the Right. Hon. Mackenzie King, who said:
I believe that whoever has made any study of public finances will consider that a system providing that one organization levies taxes and another spend the money thus obtained is entirely wrong. In other words, paying subsidies to the provinces without their having to collect taxes on their own will not lead to the careful control over expenditures which would be exercised if the provinces had, in the first place, to find the money themselves. It is a bad system, one that is altogether wrong.
Those two testimonies should be enough to convince the most timid minds. They only add to the general complaints made by most provincial prime ministers, who, during federal-provincial conferences, ceased to demand, for their legislatures, the fiscal rights of which they were deprived in 1917 and 1942 by the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, it was easier for the former government to destroy the constitutional pact. It is also, at this time, much more difficult to reconstitute the confederative pact, but I have great hopes that the Minister of Finance will make some contribution to this end. As a matter of fact, following negotiations between the premier of Quebec and himself, he also proved and recognized that the situation had to be settled before proceeding with the redistribution of provincial or federal rights.
I should like to pay tribute to the Minister of Finance who, in co-operation with the present Quebec premier, has settled that problem.
Mr. Chairman, the provinces have long been demanding restitution of the rights from which they have been dispossessed.

And they will go on demanding restoration of those rights until justice has been done. No province would ever think of preventing the federal government from fulfilling its tasks but, on the other hand, all of them wish to fulfil theirs, without any external interference.
To deprive a man from his fortune and then to offer him charity is not honest, and we will not accept such a deal. According to us, it is time the federal authorities-and once again I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance for having initiated such an approach-should become fully aware that the federal government does not have all powers, nor a monopoly on the exercise of those powers. The rights of all concerned have been clearly defined, so let each party conform, and have regard for their respective rights and powers.
Some governments may have been inclined to consider right what was wrong, and honest what was not, but we cannot, in good conscience, allow such a situation to go on. Once again, we must fully understand that we are not speaking only as citizens of the province of Quebec, and I know that the other provinces are of the same opinion, especially those that were deprived of their rights and whose wealth has been taken away from them.
Mr. Chairman, I therefore believe that it is up to our government to assume its responsibilities and to give unto Caesar what is Caesar's and unto the provinces what rightfully belongs to them.
Much was said about the equalization system and the mitigated reimbursement formula, in the form of grants for educational purposes. Again I repeat to the hon. member for Gatineau that the word "grant" means strings attached; there is a big difference between "grant" and "gift".
We are quite prepared to admit that the federal government has a role to play in the intellectual and scientific education of the people, but as the responsibility for education belongs, first of all, to the family and not to the state, so are educational responsibilities primarily of a provincial rather than of a federal character. To make a gift is one way to silence whiners, but it is not the way to correct an injustice. Let us not forget the saying: "Let us beware of the Greeks even when they are bearing gifts."
Even if we set aside all economic considerations about tax sharing arrangements, we must remember that it is one aspect only of the relations between the federal govern-
Dominion-Provincial Relations ment and the provinces that we must consider, and once again, to repeat words which our opponents could not question since they are those of Hon. Ernest Lapointe:
The federal power is the offspring, not the father, of the provinces.
It must be fully realized that relations between the provinces and the federal government cannot indefinitely stand such wrangling. Federal-provincial conferences have accomplished little progress, and it is with some misgivings that we look to the day when one or several provinces, dissatisfied at being treated as poor relatives by their big brother in Ottawa, will decide to go their own way.
However, nothing is eternal in this world, and I would not like to contribute to a split within the confederative family. Yet, I must recognize that the provinces have some very definite rights for which the federal government has not always shown proper respect in the past. But I know the present government is deeply respectful of provincial rights and will always strive-as it has been doing since it took office-to settle the many problems which were created in large part by the former administration. It must not be forgotten, Mr. Chairman, that it would be much easier for Quebec and Ontario to do without confederation than for confederation to do without them.
We must at all costs avoid letting the matter of fiscal relations become a cause of serious misunderstanding, and to that end, we must re-establish proper balance and reinstate justice.
Mr. Chairman, allow me, in closing my remarks, to publicly commend, on behalf of the constituency of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, the present Minister of Finance who, more than anyone else in the past, has been striving to work out a solution to this problem. The present Minister of Finance has not assumed a take it or leave it attitude. He has had frank discussions with the authorities of the Quebec government. I want to commend him publicly for it, and say to him that in co-operation with the Prime Minister of Canada, his actions have served to strengthen national unity, rather than to weaken it, as was the case under the former administration.
I was very sorry to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Gatineau. He has attacked a fondly regretted man, the Hon.

As I said at the outset of my remarks, he was one of the first to denounce the centralizing attitude of the former government. Gradually, the governments of every province gave their support to the stand taken by the Hon. Maurice Duplessis. The Hon. Maurice Duplessis has now entered history, and on behalf of the constituents of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, I lay a wreath of gratitude on his grave.
The late lamented Hon. Paul Sauve wanted to take over where the Hon. Maurice Duplessis had left off, but unfortunately death came to him too early. Mr. Chairman, we have as leader of the province of Quebec an authentic worker who still holds his union membership card. It is fitting that an authentic labour man like Mr. Barrette should solve this problem in co-operation with the Minister of Finance. I can assure the minister that the province of Quebec is happy about the decision concerning this agreement, and the province of Quebec breathes freely again.
Under the former government, the province of Quebec was held in a yoke; it was a matter of "take it or leave it". It was not democratic; there was no discussion with the province of Quebec. It was true dictature. I believe the Minister of Finance, by discussing frankly this problem, has served the cause of democracy and restored the people of Quebec and the people of Canada's confidence in our democratic principles.

Mr. Chairman, the C.C.F., of course, is going to support this resolution with a great deal of pleasure, especially the first part having to do with a way of extending grants to educational institutions.
When I was at university, Mr. Chairman, taking history there was a very strong emphasis on Canadian history; and one of the O.K. phrases that was always being thrown at us and that we were supposed to pay a great deal of attention to was what you might call bonne ententeism; or, if you want the O.K. phrase in the political vernacular, which has been fashionable for so long in the country, national unity. When I listen ito a speech such as I have just heard-I must confess through the translation system-and hear someone talking about "our" constitution, I wonder whether bonne ententeism has not gone a little too far; because there are conceptions of the constitution other than what I think was the rather selfish and narrow interpretation which has just been put on it by the last speaker.
I would like to say there is always a possibility of misunderstanding. I would also like to say there are other views of Cana-dianism, there are other people who are proud of Canada, and there are other people who have interpretations of the constitution and beliefs in the constitution that may differ markedly.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I would like to start with something that has been called by the newspapers the "Churchill thesis". The Churchill thesis does not refer to the great Winston Churchill but to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Churchill thesis in a nutshell, as I understand it from press reports of a few years ago, was that it was possible to form a federal government in this country without worrying too much about the Quebec vote. It seems to me that

this government, led by the Prime Minister, achieved that result in a sweeping victory in 1958. It had 200-plus seats. It really did not need its Quebec supporters, and those of us who noted the Churchill thesis have been watching ever since to see the moves that were made that would indicate the relationship and the attitude of this particular government toward Quebec. Many of us have lamented, and perhaps have pin-pointed, the fact that so far there has not seemed to emerge any striking attitude toward Quebec other than indifference. There is weak Quebec cabinet representation. There do not seem to be too many concessions.
It seems to me that this move by the Minister of Finance-and I think he deserves much congratulation-indicates that this government is pushing on with the Churchill thesis. I know he can probably argue-I believe he did-from a number of quotations that this new arrangement that is being entered into with Quebec is nothing startling; that it is consistent with the government's position that this government will not encroach upon any provincial autonomy or provincial jurisdiction in the field of education. Whether it is a legal marriage or a common law relationship, it seems to me that we now have a situation where in the field of university education the last of the 10 blocks has been moved. When you interweave the tax structure and the financial structure we have in Canada as between the provinces and the dominion government, all the complications of formula that the minister has produced cannot conceal that as far as my interpretation goes-the minister may not agree with this-this is a break-through.
We have had a number of break-throughs and a very inconsistent pattern, but for many years the Quebec government has tacitly accepted a variety of invasions of its so-called jurisdiction in education. We all know of examples in the vocational field and so far as technical training is concerned. This goes way back to the royal commission established before the first war. I remember that a writer for the Montreal Star, Tim Creery, had three articles on this matter a year ago this month, and he had a long list of examples where Quebec had accepted assistance. Even Mr. Duplessis, with all his pride in autonomy, never returned to the federal government the money he took in the first year the university grants were in operation, which is the kind of compromise of consistency that I think indicates a trend as to where we are going.
As I say, I feel that this is a great breakthrough, and I think the minister deserves congratulations because one of the things that
Dominion-Provincial Relations bother a great many people in Canada who do not live adjacent to or among or with French Canadians is a feeling that somehow they insist in taking a different view of Canadianism and of what Canadians want and need from that of people within the rest of the country. This is a most delicate and touchy subject for a politician to confront, but I think it needs some confronting. Like many other members who have come here in the last few years, while I had read a great deal in Canadian history about the French-Canadian problem, it was not until I began to follow the French-Canadian newspapers with more intensity that I realized the markedly different conception of Canadianism that the French Canadians have. This, it seems to me, is something that we very much need to resolve even in the name of that magical phrase, national unity.
One feeling I have taken from reading the French-Canadian press is that they have what is almost a conceit in their Canadianism. They push upon other Canadians an interpretation that I cannot accept and which I think many members of the house cannot accept. It seems that the contradistinction between their kind of Canadianism and ours is that theirs is French Canadian based upon language and Roman Catholic based upon religion and so on the other hand we have to be Protestant and English speaking. I do not think this necessarily holds true.
I know that in my constituency we have very few French Canadians. We have a good many Catholics who in the main are English speaking. Many of them in descent are Italians, Poles, and so on. I do not think their conception of Canadianism has to take a back seat at any time to what I might call the superiority complex of Canadianism that exists in French Canada-
That is not so.
-especially as you find it in the newspapers.
That is not so.

Some hon. member has said "That is not so". I am sure he will have the opportunity to get up and rebut what I say. I am giving my own interpretation.
The last speaker mentioned the compact theory of government or constitution that is set out in the Tremblay report. I do not know how many English speaking members of the house have read the Tremblay report, but it is a rather scary document in terms of the kind of Canadianism that I think I share with quite a number of Canadians. The main basis of the report is that the constitution is a solemn compact or treaty and, even

Dominion-Provincial Relations more, it is argued by some that the government at Ottawa is the creature of the provinces which brought about confederation. An element of this thinking creeps into the Tremblay report. I should like to refer to the main premises of the report as summarized in a book entitled "Evolving Canadian Federalism" by A. R. M. Lower and Frank Scott. They are as follows:
1.	The primary purpose of Canadian federalism is to allow the two great cultural communities which make up our population (a) to live and develop themselves according to their respective particularisms and, (b) to co-operate in the building and progress of a common fatherland.
2.	With regard to French-Canadian culture, the province of Quebec assumes alone the responsibilities which the other provinces jointly assume with regard to Anglo-Canadian culture.
For the benefit of the member who interrupted, the basis for my remarks is found in the words I have just read, to wit:
With regard to French-Canadian culture, the province of Quebec assumes alone the responsibilities which the other provinces jointly assume with regard to Anglo-Canadian culture.
The hon. member is long on theory but short on facts.

I continue.
3.	The Canadian reality, both economic and sociological, has undergone a profound transformation since 1867, but its cultural elements have not changed, so that the basic problem still remains the same.
The authors continue:
Thus posed, the postulates, formulated without any consultation with representatives from outside Quebec, lead on to a critical analysis of present trends toward centralization and call for a "readaptation of the public administration according to the spirit of federalism".
Obviously this is a type of federalism that most of us in -the rest of the country do not appreciate. It seems to me that one place where politicians fail lamentably is in being candid and honest in this particular field. Everybody wants to wrap cotton wool around this very difficult problem, and it seems to me that in this particular case where we have a concession, where we have a move forward, we should put it bluntly that we think this is an excellent move, a move away from the Tremblay report position which the previous speaker extolled as being the epitome of Duplessisism, toward the kind of Canadian-ism in which I think the rest of the country believes. If you push the Tremblay report position too far it seems to me you have a situation not unlike that of the security council of the United Nations, in that Quebec always has the right of veto just as Russia always seems to have the right of veto in the security council. The same thing seems to apply with respect to the constitutional interpretation of many people in Quebec.
[Mr. Fisher.1
They believe in a separatism, with Quebec always having the right of veto over proposals from other provinces or the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, before the
luncheon hour I was trying to deal with a delicate subject, and one in which I never claimed to be an authority. There are many other hon. members in this house who can speak with more authority than I can on French-Canadian relations with the rest of the country. I detest the use of the expression English-Canadians but I am going to refer to French-Canadian relations with Canadians. However, this compromise that has been worked out by the Minister of Finance is an important break-through in these relations and is one that I think we should assess in some detail.
One of the things that has intrigued me has been the tremendous amount of involvement and the federal build-up in recent years in the field of education. Last year the newspaperman to whom I referred, Tim Creery, worked through the estimates and in a series of articles that appeared on March 2, 3 and 4, 1959, in the Montreal Star, he traced the scope of federal aid in the matter of education. His estimate, and this was confirmed in his talks with statisticians in the dominion bureau of statistics, was that approximately $100 million would be spent on education by the federal government, making it a very large contributor and financially comparable directly with all but three of the provinces in this responsibility.
In his article of March 3 he listed the estimated departmental spending on education for the year April 1, 1959 to March 31, 1960. The first was the Department of Finance, through the university grants, totalling $26,221,000; second, the Canada Council scholarships and grants, roughly $1.5 million and then, for capital construction under the Canada Council, $6 million; citizenship and immigration, Indian affairs branch, for operation and maintenance, approximately $13,734,000 and for plant, well over $7 million. The same department spends approximately $400,000 for its 50 per cent share of citizenship and language instruction. The department of northern affairs spends a total of approximately $9 million on education in the territories, that is for both direct education and maintenance and also for employment.

The Department of Labour makes payments to the provinces under the apprenticeship training and vocational and technical schools assistance of approximately $9.5 million; national defence, through the three service colleges, the naval venture plan, and regular officers training plan, spends approximately $6 million. The Department of Trade and Commerce, through national research council scholarships and grants in aid of research spends about $8 million. The atomic energy control board spends about $650,000 in scholarships. The Department of Transport, through its schools of navigation and seamanship, steamship inspection service, radio operators training, aviation instruction, and so on, spends approximately $600,000. The Department of National Health and Welfare, through its national health grants, education proportion must spend approximately $1 million. The Department of Veterans Affairs is in the field of education through correspondence courses, $29,000; vocational and technical training, $55,000; university training $49,000; and children of the war dead, $481,000. The Department of Agriculture spends, on grants in aid of agricultural research, $187,000; mines and technical surveys, through its grants in aid of geological research in Canadian universities, spends $50,000; University of British Columbia, for research in foreign geography, $3,500. The last two departments contributing to education are fisheries, contributions to research, $25,000 and scholarships, $25,000, and external affairs, NATO fellowships and studies, $42,000.
All this totals roughly just under $100 million which was spent last year in what almost everyone will agree was a proper federal activity in the field of education. However, if Quebec thesis or the Tremblay report thesis or the Pigeon thesis is correct in so far as this situation is concerned, such expenditures were wrong and unconstitutional. If their interpretation is correct, then Quebec should be fighting this much more wholeheartedly than has been the case. I think, if I remember correctly, Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent engineered two of the largest contributions in this federal program, that is the university grants and the Canada Council scholarships and capital construction grants. This is an indication to me that the Tremblay report, and the understanding that it represents is anachronistic, it is out of time, that Quebec is past the Tremblay stage.
There is a much more definite move in Quebec toward a realization that education is a field in which the federal government is properly working. I do not feel we will ever get an improved educational system in Canada unless and until this whole matter
Dominion-Provincial Relations of provincial jurisdiction becomes less a matter of controversy and much more a matter of co-operation and co-ordination for the greater good of all. I have said before in this house, and I am sure many hon. members agree, that you are not a Quebecer, or an Ontarian, a Manitoban or a British Columbian, but you are a Canadian.
You are a Canadian first.
Nowhere does this apply more than in the field of education. I notice I am getting interruptions again from the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.
You are very long on theory but rather short on practice.
I know the hon. member is very practical. I understand he changed overnight from being a Liberal to a Conservative.
I am proud of it.

May I suggest that the thoughts of one of the leading spokesmen for that kind of trend in Quebec and French Canada and of other Canadians who are interested in the problem were expressed by Maurice Lamontagne who, as I think all hon. members know, has an association, if indirectly, with this House of Commons. He argued in this way or at least this is the interpretation put upon it by Frank R. Scott interpreting Mr. Lamontagne's book "The Canadian Federalism" published in 1954. According to Frank Scott, Mr. Lamontagne states:
For him the only solution for Quebec is "a lucid integration into the new Canadian federalism."
Mr. Scott goes on to say this:
This solution, as has been shown, is repudiated expressly and at length in the Tremblay report. But the commissioners themselves admit that the far-reaching decentralization they advocate cannot be brought about immediately, because "de facto situations and habits of thought have been created which must be corrected," and they therefore offer a "temporary solution" which confines itself to a mere reallocation of taxes within the present constitutional scheme. That some such financial adjustments will be made in the future is probable; no part of the Canadian constitution has been more flexible, more responsive to changing political and economic pressures, than the subsidies provisions and tax arrangements. But the profound reshaping of the constitution itself, called for in the main recommendations of this report, is another matter. It cannot be as divorced, as it is here, from the hard facts of Canada's increasing industrial growth in an increasingly dangerous world. The preservation of human and cultural values in this day and age, which this report professes to seek, is an aim all Canadians would support; what would be questioned, in Quebec as outside, is the possibility of reverting to smaller governmental units, however distinct they may be in race or religion, for the almost exclusive protection of those values. The present distribution of powers in Canada has not satisfied everyone,

Dominion-Provincial Relations but it has unquestionably permitted a wide freedom for the steady development of the two cultural groups along their own distinctives lines.
Complementary to those remarks or that interpretation, I go along with and interpret the move the minister has succeeded in making in this regard as another step along this particular path.
Before lunch we heard from the hon. member for Bellechasse and, as a result of a question put to him by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, he argued that Quebec has an obligation to French Canadians in the rest of Canada. This is an argument that seems to me to be most controversial. If Quebec has an obligation to French Canadians in the rest of Canada, as a government, surely it has an obligation to that diaspora of French Canadians in the New England states. I am sure these lost ones should arouse the same reaction among French Canadians in Quebec. If Quebec has an obligation for French Canadians in the rest of Canada, what about English Canadians in the rest of Canada and their obligations to English Canadians in Quebec? I have yet to encounter a provincial authority anywhere outside of Quebec that would follow along with this argument.
It seems to me that this assumption by the hon. member for Bellechasse expressed in governmental terms on the part of the province would look forward to a continuation of strife throughout the rest of Canadian history. Then a provincial government, according to this argument, has the obligation to go into the rest of Canada to further the particular ethnic and cultural problems of French Canadians or English Canadians in the rest of Canada. It certainly seems to me to be a most controversial argument.
In so far as the second part of the resolu-is concerned, it merely continues the 13 per cent rate the minister introduced several years ago. Some of the provinces have been asking for an increase. The minister has brought down a budget that envisages a sound, constructive balance and obviously this resolution is merely geared to it. Today in almost every municipality it is fashionable to look toward the provincial authority and cry for more; and we know it is fashionable for provincial authorities to look toward the federal government and to cry for more. The way out of the jack-pot undoubtedly will be found on a very empirical basis or through a shading of development rather than in a clear, new rewriting of tax agreements or tax proposals.
To refer to the problem that develops from the first part of this resolution, namely the field of education, one can certainly see


where there needs to be a wide new understanding of the entire problem. One of the disappointing things about the federal House of Commons to anyone who has been involved in education and who finds as he goes around the country that education is a live issue, is that here it is not a live issue. I think two hon. members from Toronto who are members of the government are the only ones of whom 1 know who have ever, in the two years I have been here in parliament, devoted major efforts to this particular field. One would almost assume that this particular parliament is not interested in education. Yet out in the municipalities and in the communities from which we come, this matter in financial terms is the most live topic of all.
I think most hon. members from Ontario will recognize the storm that has arisen just in the last few weeks over the new tax grant brought down by the province of Ontario. Of course it seems to me that the argument of the premier of Ontario is that no real changes or advances will be possible in the immediate future unless there is some support from the federal government first. What the way out of this difficulty is, I do not know. I think this is the toughest problem faced by the minister as Minister of Finance.
However, I am certainly convinced, as is our party, that this is one field in which federal support must be ready and be more available than it has been in the past in the way of more funds in order that the provincial governments can accept their educational load. Of course this raises the question whether there should be any consignment or direction of funds from the federal government to the provinces, that is as to how they are spent. I do not think any of us have reached the stage where we are prepared to argue favourably that question but I think we shall eventually be obliged to arrive at it if we want to get in Canada the standard of education or health we need.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to reiterate our group's support of this resolution and to congratulate the Minister of Finance for moving or shaping Quebec a little bit along the path towards greater co-operation with the rest of Canada. I know he may disclaim credit for such a move or at least our interpretation of that move; but I think he deserves it. I must give credit not only to him but to those hon. members from Quebec who obviously have changed their position to quite an extent. If they are able to vote in support of this particular resolution, it seems to me that I and even those who have looked at the Tremblay report can forget all about that now that

they are moving along the path toward a different kind of Canadianism from that which seems to have been popular in Quebec in recent years.

This legislation of the province of Quebec has made possible the establishment of a special sinking fund for building projects of our Quebec universities. We are informed that at present a special $75 million fund covers those Quebec universities building projects.

Mr. Chairman, that is a good result of this legislation, that is a practical result, and that is why we, members from Quebec, we who are in the federal field, are happy to commend the government and urge it to continue in the right direction, that of respecting-as it has done and with what solicitude, since it came to power-the rights of all the ethnic groups in Canada and in all the provinces

It is for this reason that we of Quebec are today happy to see that the government of this province will be able to supply the necessary funds to its universities and institutions of higher learning.
