Mr. Chairman, I also would like to make a few brief remarks, not as unpleasant as those the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) would like to make them, but some remarks about this resolution.
This matter of tax sharing to provide alternative arrangement for the payment of grants to our institutions of higher learning has been much discussed and has raised much controversy. It is a matter which has been much discussed by the population of the province of Quebec and about which the province had given its full support to the premier of that time, the hon. Mr. Duplessis, who will be well remembered by the whole country as one of the greatest premiers of French Canada.
We are about to settle this matter which had no other fate than being put off from time to time by the former Liberal federal government. And it is significant that this question should be settled by the ministers and the members who form the present Conservative government.
Mr. Chairman, if you analyse the factors involved in the agreement about to be concluded between the government of Quebec on the one hand and the central government on the other, it is obvious that one of the main causes of this success is the totally different attitude of the present government as compared to that of the previous gov-


ernment. The arrogant, intractable take it or leave it attitude has been replaced by a friendly, understanding attitude and by a desire to settle a problem which concerns one of Canada's most beautiful provinces: the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, the man who occupied the chair a moment ago knows better than anyone, because of his background, that the city of St. Hyacinthe is famous for its contribution to education throughout the country. He knows that our educational institutions are a credit not only to St. Hyacinthe, but to the whole country. Each year, in St. Hyacinthe, students from everywhere in Canada, and even from the United States and other countries, come to acquire the knowledge that will make of them qualified men in their respective fields.
I seize this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to say a well deserved tribute to our educational institutions and, in particular, to their teaching staff. By their conduct and their knowledge, the teachers helped make prominent citizens of our people, and this even well beyond our frontiers.
I am sure of expressing the feeling of our people, Mr. Chairman, when paying tribute to two great Quebec figures, men who have done so much for the progress of education in our province. I am referring toi Hon. Maurice Duplessis and Hon. Paul Sauve, former premiers of Quebec. As you know,'/ both have greatly contributed to the agreement which we are about to adopt. It was the realistic and logical position of these two premiers, who had the entire and immediate support of the Quebec population which paved the way for the agreement now before us. To the first, we owe our gratitude for his tenacity and his steadfast stand against those who wanted him to accept proposals which went against the best interests of the province of Quebec. Deeply convinced that Quebec, on account of its faith, tongue and traditions, is not a province like the others, he has always insisted upon such an approach to the problems. That is what the present Minister of Finance understood, after the present Prime Minister, Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. The record has amply justified premier Duplessis' attitude, since he was, at the start, the only one to rise against the Liberal government of the time and now practically all the premiers of the other provinces have

accepted his opinions and taken the same attitude as he did. To my knowledge-
You have forgotten Drew.

To my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, premier Duplessis is the man who launched the agreement that we are definitely reaching. The second one, Hon. Paul Sauve, whom the Liberals recognize today as a great Canadian from Quebec, most probably because he is now dead-for when he was in power, they had started a petty campaign of slander against him, as they had always done with regard to his predecessor. Hon. Paul Sauve is certainly to be considered the architect of the present agreement. His wish to serve his people, his way of looking at things objectively and realistically and his broadmindedness were at the basis of the present agreement. He too deserves our never-ending gratitude, as well as that of the other citizens of this country.
Another great promoter of the present understanding is the present premier of Quebec, Hon. Antonio Barrette. A gentleman of politics, as he is called-
Not by us.

-because of his tact, his patriotism, his politeness-which is totally lacking in the hon. member for Dollard- and his realism, brought together all people of good will who wished a practical solution for all concerned. We owe him also our most sincere gratitude.
As a Conservative member, Mr. Chairman-
You mean as a Union Nationale member.

Yes, as a supporter of the Union Nationale, and I am proud to proclaim it, because it is a government which has done much for the province of Quebec; it is a government which has had also the support of the people of the province of Quebec, in spite of all the slanderous and stifling influences of the Liberal party against everything it was doing.
I feel a very legitimate pride, as a Conservative member, in having taken part in this understanding, and of having done something to bring it to the point-
Of being completed.

-of being completed since this will be a monument to the glory of the
Dominion-Provincial Relations Conservative party and will make desperation of the Grits, those wet blankets. I am certainly glad for having done something about it for it is an important and definite step that will certainly, as I just said, be a monument to the glory of the Conservative party. The Minister of Finance who never ceased working for ensuring justice to all concerned also deserves all our gratitude. The difficulties he faced at various times did not break the indomitable courage which is so characteristic of him. He has also continued to work towards a final agreement. The people of Quebec see in him, and they have seen it for quite a while, one of their closest friends.
We must also recognize that our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker has done a lot to bring about that agreement. He is the worthy successor of the right hon. Sir John A. Macdonald, since he is following in his footsteps in order to assure everywhere an integral Canadianism from sea to sea.
Mr. Chairman, certain statements made in this house or elsewhere lead to believe that in the province of Quebec nothing, or almost nothing, was done for the furtherance of schooling and education. I should like at this point, Mr. Chairman, to give some figures which can certainly clear up, in the minds of right-minded people-but not of some of those to my left-
Name them.
-because they have never been able to understand anything, they are simply imbued with-
He does not know his left.
They have a bitter taste in their mouth that comes from losing the power. It is only with spite, remorse and resentment that they speak and reveal what is on their minds.
Rumilly will be shocked.

This house is surely interested in knowing that early in 1959, the province of Quebec had the largest number of university students. Out of a total population of 4,884,000, there were in that province 29,320 students entitled to federal assistance. That is 5,324 more students than in Ontario for the same year.
Mr. Chairman, if we consider that from 1945 to 1959 inclusive, the Quebec government has appropriated the fabulous sum of $768,706,931.34 for public education, it is impossible not to rejoice at the results the

Dominion-Provincial Relations measure before us will bring about. With more money, the Quebec government will, under the able leadership of its present premier, the Hon. Antonio Barrette-who will also be premier after the next election -do a still better job in the province in the field of education and teaching.
In June 1959, during the annual convention of learned societies of this country which was held in Saskatoon, Miss Rosemary Bushell, of the research bureau of the conference of Canadian universities and colleges, stated that among Canadian governments, the Quebec government was giving the greatest help to universities and their students. In the academic year 1956-1957, the Quebec government contributed in a proportion of 54 per cent to student aid throughout Canada, in the form of fellowships and scholarships.
If, Mr. Chairman, we make the comparison between the years 1943-1944, under a Liberal government, and 1957-1958, it will be found that amounts earmarked for university teaching in the province of Quebec, rose from $2,356,000 to $14,570,460, that is, an increase of 600 per cent.
(Text):
Shame on the Grits. (Translation):

Such are, Mr. Chairman, the figures I challenge hon. members on the Liberal benches to question. I have quoted them in this house to make the Liberals still more sorry, as you cannot fail to realize, Mr. Chairman, that since the legislation is before us, deep gloom has gripped the ranks of the Liberal party.
Finally, there is a point which we have not been able to solve, Mr. Chairman. During the 20 years they were in power, the question remained pending, and it shall be settled by the Conservative party, to the benefit of those among our people who really want educational advancement.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the way the Conservative government wants to administer things. Indeed, we are always feeling the pulse of the working population and keeping close to it, because the workers are keeping close to us. They have put their trust in us and will never stop trusting us.
The hon. member spoke differently when the Hon. Duplessis was still living.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express a few thoughts that came to my mind about the two or three speeches I have heard today. First of all, I was hurt,-and I say so dispassionately,- to hear the hon. member for Port Arthur,

(Mr. Fisher) whom I hold in high esteem, speaking as he did of the province of Quebec and its people.
Sure enough, there are fanatics and bigots in the province of Quebec, as in the nine other provinces, but they are not very many.
The province of Quebec is conscious, at least all right-minded people are, that we form part of the Canadian confederation. We understand that Canadian citizens, whether they live in Prince Edward Island, in Newfoundland, in Manitoba or in Ontario, are Canadian just as much as we are, and that we are Canadian just as much as they are.
I really regret that the hon. member for Port Arthur should have spoken the way he did today in this house.
He used to be a Liberal.

He certainly did not do so with a view to promoting good understanding in this country. If he took the trouble of visiting our province, not only for two days, but for a whole week end in Quebec city or in Montreal, and of associating with us, exchanging ideas with us, he would no doubt change his mind about the citizens of the province of Quebec.
There is another argument I should like to adduce in support of what I have just said, and it is that all citizens of the province of Quebec should not be judged by the views of some people who, from time to time, may have expressed very personal ideas which do not represent the general thinking of the population of Quebec.
I should be interested to know what Mr. Claude Jodin will say and what Mr. Michel Chartrand will think of the ideas expressed this morning by the hon. member for Port Arthur.
In any event, I should like to assure him of the friendship of the citizens of Quebec, and I invite him to come to our province and to associate with us. He would soon realize that we are as good Canadians as he is and as are all other Canadians of the other provinces.
It must not be forgotten that he is an advanced Liberal.

Mr. Chairman, I also listened carefully to what was said by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard); in his speech, he made an admission of which I should like to remind him.
He told us that the former premier, the Hon. Paul Sauve-for whom I have never hidden my esteem,-was the originator of this agreement, because he had shown objectivity and realism.

Would that mean, by any chance, that his predecessor had shown no objectivity nor realism in the discussion of those matters?
We have been told that the Liberal administration had neither the courage nor the brains to settle the university question. However, the door was always left open in Ottawa for discussing this problem.
There was a screen.

We always got the same answers, it was always the same negative attitude. I repeat to my hon. friends -and I say with no ill feelings whatsoever-* because if I recall these facts to the weak memory of our hon. friends from Quebec, it is because, as the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) pointed out, I think today's legislation is a clear testimony to the memory and glory of Mr. St. Laurent. I join in with all my colleagues to pay him tribute. However, I do not want it to be only in my own words, but I would like to quote in support an excerpt from the Globe and Mail, a newspaper which is not particularly close to the Liberal party. Part of an editorial from this newspaper was quoted in l'Action Catholique lor Friday, September 24, 1954, and I quote:
Such is also the opinion of the Toronto Globe and Mail-
The article had just quoted another newspaper:
Such is also the opinion of the Toronto Globe and Mail, which believes that Mr. St. Laurent's speech will go down in Canada's history. The article then goes on to take a pot shot at the premier of Quebec.
And here is the quotation from the Globe and Mail:
We are quite sure that Mr. Duplessis never intended to start something so constructive. He was merely indulging in politics. But he pushed it to the point where Mr. St. Laurent was forced to answer back, and in his reply, he reached one of the highest levels of statesmanship.
This morning, the hon. member for Cham-bly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) challenged the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) to prove that university rectors had spoken up when it was very slyly suggested to them that they were not to accept the grants to universities. I have here a clipping from La Presse for November 14, 1956, which bears the title:
Mr. St. Laurent's offer to the universities is unanimously carried.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
Let me quote the first paragraph of this article:
The national conference of Canadian universities has unanimously accepted the offer it has received from the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, Prime Minister of Canada, to administer and distribute the funds placed at its disposal to help Canadian universities.
Mr. Chairman, I draw attention to the next sentence:
The representative of the province of Quebec was one of the members of both the finance committee and the executive committee of the conference who took a stand on this matter.
And further on, in an item entitled: "Mgr. Lussier takes a definite stand", I read:
I obey to what seems to me to be a conscience duty and I state strongly our respect for the federal and provincial authority. I think I can state, said the rector, that under the circumstances described, the money that is offered could be accepted for capital expenditures.
The rector of the University of Montreal, Mgr. Irenee Lussier, adopted a truly vigorous stand when he gave his opinion on the acceptance of federal assistance to higher education, without the approbation of his council of governors. As we all know, the council of governors of the University of Montreal includes persons who are in one way or another answerable to the government of the province of Quebec, which places the rector in a delicate situation when it comes to state a truly academic policy.
A little further on, and this is the last sentence I want to quote dealing with the financial situation of the university, Mgr. Lussier added:
That is why we suffer at this time from being in a situation which seems to force us to make an apparently political choice.
Mr. Chairman, I believe this is clear enough, and I am not making up anything. This was published in La Presse of November 14, 1956, and those are the very words of the rector of the University of Montreal, Mgr. Irenee Lussier.
Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that we will support wholeheartedly this resolution. As did some Conservative members from Quebec,
I want to pay a tribute to Mr. Sauve for having had the intelligence to make constructive and concrete proposals to the federal government.
The only reproach we can make to the former premier of Quebec is that in the field of grants to universities, he always said no, closed the door and walked away. I believe Mr. Sauve acted like a great Canadian in coming here to explain to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to the Minister

Dominion-Provincial Relations of Finance (Mr. Fleming) the proposal of the province of Quebec, and in believing that we had no right to deprive of high school and university education, as the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville said, a whole generation of young people.
Mr. Chairman, I said I would not speak for a long time. I close my remarks in saying that we are going to vote with much enthusiasm in favour of the bill which will be introduced after this resolution. We only regret that, in Quebec, it took so long to understand that the duty of a public man is to see, first of all, to the general welfare of the community, before thinking about the re-election of his party and his followers. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry? The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
What does he know about Quebec?

Mr. Chairman, I understood one of the hon. members to ask as I rose in my seat, what did I know about Quebec? I know quite a little bit about Quebec, and I have known quite a little bit about Quebec for a very long time.
I was rather astonished at some of the things said by the hon. member for Port Arthur this afternoon, who admitted that only since 1957 when he was elected to this house had he begun to make any serious study of French Canada and on the basis of the three years' elementary course that he had taken, of the affairs of one third of this country, he proceeded to pontificate this afternoon.
I do think that there are some of us who have had a longer time to observe our fellow citizens in Quebec and in other parts of Canada where they speak the French language than apparently has been the case with the hon. member for Port Arthur. I think if the hon. member for Port Arthur, who is a very intelligent member and I think a man of good will-I would not contest that for one minute-and who is also constantly talking about the history of this country, had just reflected on the history of this country in this twentieth century and had been asked, "If you had to pick three men out of all the Canadians who have taken a part in public affairs in this twentieth century, three men who had contributed as much as any other three men to a recognition that this is a country with two equal cultures and a country where citizens, whatever their origin, are equal, who would you pick?", those three men would have been Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Ernest Lapointe and Louis St. Laurent.

I do not say that you could not pick three other names equally worthy, and there is certainly one which I would say was in every respect equally worthy, Mr. Mackenzie King. But I would draw attention to the fact-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What about Premier Smallwood? Where would you put him?

The hon. member for Saint John-Albert, who is seizing one of those rather rare occasions when I speak to make a speech himself, asks me where I would put the premier of Newfoundland. I will tell him where I would put the premier of Newfoundland: the premier of Newfoundland thought so much of this country when Louis St. Laurent was prime minister that he brought Newfoundland into Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I would hope that the hon. member would get back to education and this resolution at some time.

I would draw your attention, sir, to the fact that I have not mentioned anything which has not been mentioned by previous speakers in this debate who have not been called to order, and I hope Your Honour will give me the same latitude as has been given to other hon. members because I have no intention to do anything in this intervention other than discuss speeches which have already been made in this debate.
I was discussing the speech made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, who spent a great deal of his time suggesting that because a few people in the province of Quebec took a rather narrow view of Canadianism, just as there are a few people in the city of Toronto and in some other parts of this country who think that they, too, have a monopoly on Canadianism, they are not very representative of French Canada, or indeed of any other part of Canada. I was pointing out that it was perhaps no accident that when one picks four names, as I did, all those four happened to be members of the Liberal party of Canada. Incidentally, the only name which was suggested from the other side was another member of the Liberal party of Canada, a man who helped to complete that dream of confederation which Sir John Macdonald joined with George Brown and a great many other Liberals in bringing about nearly a century ago.
I was also rather astonished to hear several hon. members sitting over on this side of the house but not in this party suggesting

that there was something rigid and intransigent about the attitude of the government which was in office when Mr. St. Laurent was prime minister. But I was very pleased to observe that that attitude was not taken by the hon. member for Bellechasse, who speaks after thinking instead of before thinking as seems to be the case with some hon. members supporting the government sitting to my immediate left. The hon. member for Bellechasse, in speaking in this debate the other day on the subject which is now before us, had this to say, as reported on page 2241 of Hansard for March 18 last:
(Translation):
Last year, I had the opportunity-as I also did during my election campaign-to say how much I had admired the gesture of the Hon. Louis St. Laurent who, after having found opposition in Quebec, and being aware that this opposition was due to a firm wish to observe the constitution, agreed, after a meeting with the Hon. Maurice Duplessis, to increase from 5 to 10 per cent the individual income tax deduction, so that provinces wishing to do so, and more particularly the province of Quebec, might exercise their own jurisdiction in the taxation field.
(Text):
That is the rigidity which was shown by the previous government. The fact of the matter is that ever since 1957 this country has been living in the kind of world which was described by Lewis Carroll in "Through the Looking Glass and what Alice found there". Everything is reversed. Not only is the former government-this is normal in parliamentary institutions to which I take no objection-now in opposition and the former opposition now in government, but history has to be changed too. All the past has to be changed by hon. gentlemen opposite. They are not satisfied with their own achievements; they must change everything that happened before. But I am glad to say that the hon. member for Bellechasse, who seems to have somewhat more regard for the facts than some hon. members on the other side of the house, has really rather exploded that whole silly notion.
The fact of the matter is that the problem we are now considering is this. I am not now talking particularly about university grants but rather about the main problems of the division of the direct tax field between the federal parliament and provincial legislatures. This is the problem which was elucidated so well a few moments ago by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville when he cited from memory- and incidentally his memory is a lot better than that of some hon. gentlemen-the provisions of the British North America Act both in sections 91 and 92 with respect to taxation. He pointed out that far from the 79951-0-180
Dominion-Provincial Relations federal parliament ever having tried to invade the provincial field, a former provincial premier put as a preamble in his legislation a statement that was not true and not in accord with the constitution, and that the premier of Quebec regularly claimed that he had a power which under the constitution the legislature of Quebec did not have at all and that is the exclusive right to impose direct taxes.
If the former premier of Quebec had believed that-no, probably I should not say that-but if the premier of Quebec had really felt he could sustain that position in the courts, why did he not challenge the income tax? Why did he not challenge all this legislation in the courts?
If the Solicitor General really believed the things he said in this chamber when he sat on this side why did he not refuse to join the government that continues to impose an income tax? One hon. gentleman said earlier today in this debate that when Sir Thomas White proposed an income tax in 1917 it was a temporary measure for wartime. That is what Sir Thomas White said, as one hon. gentleman reminded us earlier. That is true enough but like many other temporary measures including some of the so-called temporary buildings they last quite a long time. I do not believe the Minister of Finance is going to get up and tell us that his follower is now his leader and that he is going to scrap the income tax and change his budget. In fact, far from that, he gave us a whopping addition to it only last year.
The plain fact is that there has been a marked change since 1957 in the attitude of the government of Canada toward the governments of the provinces in this field but that change is quite the opposite of what hon. gentlemen opposite said it would be when they sat over here. In 1957 the old tax rental system was coming up for revision. The agreements would have expired and did in fact expire on March 31, 1957. More than two years before that Mr. St. Laurent as prime minister of this country called the first conference to discuss this matter. Again I remind hon. gentlemen this was done two years before the impending expiry. Counting all the various meetings that were held, five meetings were held with provincial representatives before the final proposition was brought into this house by Mr. Harris in 1956. In the course of those discussions many modifications were made at the suggestion of the provincial governments.
After that long process some finality, of course, had to be reached and the legislation was brought in which was described by the

Dominion-Provincial Relations present Minister of Finance as incomprehensible. I think that is the word he used. I have Hansard here if I am challenged, but I do not think I will be. And while it is true that in the end the Tory opposition did vote for that bill, or at least did not vote against it-

I asked the minister if the opposition of that day voted against it?

speechtext: The Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act?
Yes.

Was there a division?

I had forgotten that but I accept the minister's correction gladly because it strengthens my argument. My argument is that this so-called inadequate and incomprehensible legislation is still the law of Canada and no improvement has been made except that a small dividend has been added. I suggested the other day when I spoke before, and I will not elaborate that point because I have already made it, that a small dividend was added for one reason and for one reason only and that was that the government did not get a majority in 1957 and they were going to the country again in 1958 and that they felt that this addition of 3 per cent reduction allowed in the personal income tax would be of some electoral advantage to them. I suggest that if the Conservatives had got a clear majority in the election of 1957 there would have been no change whatever in the tax-sharing arrangements act until the time of its expiry in 1962. It is very obvious that from March 31, 1958 we have had no suggestion that there would be any improvement. But, we have had some very extraordinary things said.
The Minister of Justice has turned out to be one of the greatest financial experts in this country. He went down to Newfoundland a year ago to make peace in Newfoundland and to tell the Newfoundlanders how much better off they were than they used to be and he did so in a toplofty patronizing way that was not much appreciated in Newfoundland. The hon. gentleman also went to Quebec to tell the people of that province how much better off they are now under a Conservative


government than they were under the government of Louis St. Laurent. He went to speak to the women's Conservative club in Quebec and I notice that the Ottawa Journal quoted what the minister had to say. In order to verify this I got a copy from the minister's office of the translation of his speech but this quotation from the Journal seems to be very adequate for the purpose. Here is what the hon. gentleman said:
We (the Conservative government) constantly show ourselves ready to study each problem on its merits, and there can be no doubt that to date the relations between the provincial and federal authorities are less strained than ever before.
This speech was made on November 25, 1959 and the report appeared in the Ottawa Journal of December 1. I draw attention to the fact that it was the Minister of Justice who said this. Let us just consider the evidence. This statement was made in 1959. That was the year this government repudiated the constitution of Canada and the obligations of Canada under the terms of union with Newfoundland thereby vastly improving our relations with Newfoundland, and the only two members of the Newfoundland legislature who supported this government were both defeated at the polls in the provincial election.
What has this to do with education?

An hon. gentleman asks me what this has to do with education. What we are discussing are the federal-provincial financial arrangements and a minor improvement this government-which claims it has created greater harmony and reduced strains with the provinces-claims to have made in that way.
What is the evidence? I refer to Newfoundland as an example but some people will say that is an extreme illustration. I will bring evidence from some of the other provinces. I have here a news item from the Cape Breton Post of October 16, certainly a newspaper that has never been accused of supporting the Liberal party and one which I think most people would regard as a very strong Tory paper. This is a Canadian Press story and no doubt it appeared in many other newspapers. I just happened to pick up this one. This was the day after the Minister of Finance had that meeting last October with the provincial ministers of finance and provincial treasurers. Here are what some of them said about this new state of harmony:
British Columbia's premier Bennett said "it's just what we expected" but he criticized "inane policies" of the federal government which had produced a big deficit-

Then, the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan said:
We are, of course, very unhappy about the decision. All the provinces are unhappy.
He called it a breach of faith. One could go on and quote a good many others, some of them not exactly opponents normally of the present government. I shall now quote Premier Stanfield. This is from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of the same date. Premier Stanfield, speaking of the conference, said he was not surprised that Ottawa was unable, because of the deficit financial position, to grant further moneys. He went on to say:
It does not follow logically that nothing could he done on an interim basis before the tax sharing arrangements expire in 1962.
I do not suppose from one end of the country to the other there is the head of any government that supports the government at Ottawa more than Premier Stanfield does, unless it is possibly Premier Flemming of New Brunswick. Premier Stanfield said that what the minister is proposing now is not logical. He said he hoped next year Ottawa's financial position would be sufficiently improved to permit something more to be done for the provinces during the current agreement. We are now being told nothing more is going to be done.
I might add that as you go further west you find that the complaints get a little stronger. For instance, in the Toronto Telegram we have this item:
Ottawa deaf to provinces' plea.
The provincial treasurer of Ontario, Mr. Allan, said that a tax adjustment was not only desirable but absolutely necessary. Mr. Roblin said the position of the federal government-
-indicated that if there is a federal surplus next year Ottawa will have to change its stand toward the provinces.
In the Winnipeg Tribune of October 17 we find an editorial entitled "Closed Door". Indeed, that is all the Minister of Finance has ever done. He and the Prime Minister gave a solemn promise, a solemn undertaking, in November, 1957 that they would have another federal-provincial conference in January of 1958. They broke that promise. They made a unilateral decision by telegram, and that is all that has ever happened since, except this meeting where, as the Winnipeg Tribune, one of the normally strong supporters of this government, said they closed the door.
Of course, you can hardly pick up a newspaper without reading a heading like this one. This is from the Ottawa Journal of October 20:
79951-0-180J
Dominion-Provincial Relations
Frost Attacks Ottawa
It has to do with this matter. Then, on January 5, 1960, we find this in the Toronto Star:
Frost Won't Pay Tax "Due" Ottawa
Then, on February 5, 1960, the Ottawa Journal carried this headline:
Frost Seeks Extra $100,000,000 From Federal Treasury
I could read these but everybody has read them. I am just putting these things on the record to show this wonderful harmony that has been created by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, and that latter day John the Baptist, the Minister of Justice, who goes talking about this harmony all over the country with a singular regard for the facts and the figures.
Then we find in the Toronto Telegram- and, if ever there was a newspaper that ought to be grateful to the government, it is that one, as the Minister of National Revenue I am sure will readily admit-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. member is talking about.

In the Toronto Telegram of February 25, 1960, we find the following: Queen's Park Blasts Ottawa Proposes Tit-For-Tat Taxes
Then, the Ottawa Journal of February 26 carries this heading:
Frost Stresses Need for Expansion Money
Again, Mr. Frost wants his $100 million. In the Hamilton Spectator of March 29 we find the following:
Frost Hints Tax-Sharing Demands May Broaden
In other words, he may not even be satisfied with $100 million. He says:
Ottawa's position had been unrealistic and unjust.
This is the harmony; this is what they have achieved.
Then, of course, when you go a little further west into Manitoba you find the present premier of that province who said he was modelling himself on the present Prime Minister of Canada; he was a real follower of John; where John went he was going to go. This was before he became the premier. He is also the provincial treasurer who had to encounter the Minister of Finance of this country. Here is his budget speech. I hold in my hand the Manitoba Hansard. I think hon. members ought to see what this harmony is we now have; I think hon. members ought to see what this Tory premier, who has just won a very considerable victory in that province, has to say about the measure that is now before us and about the attitude of this government. I quote from page 20 of the

Dominion-Provincial Relations budget speech, which is to be found in the Manitoba Hansard for March 17, 1960:
The problems of intergovernmental relations in the past year have bulked large on the governmental scene. There has been some progress. Hon. members will recall that, following the plenary dominion-provincial fiscal conference of November, 1957, it was expected the conference would be reconvened early in 1958 to examine fully the requirements for improvement in the financial status of the provinces.
Hon. members will see what Mr. Roblin said:
It was expected the conference would be reconvened early in 1958 to examine fully the requirements for improvement in the financial status of the provinces. This meeting did not materialize.
I suppose that is as far as a Tory can go. He means they did not carry out their promise. I continue:
It was not until midsummer of 1959 that a committee of ministers of finance and provincial treasurers met in Ottawa.
This committee, by its very nature as it became clear, could not resolve the issues at stake.
I cannot take the time of the committee to read all of this but I will read the choicest extracts. I go to page 21, and here is what he said: Here is the provincial treasurer and premier of Manitoba talking about the Minister of Finance:
Our claim for increased revenues from this source received short shrift at the hands of the Minister of Finance.
That is the way those who were going to have a new regime of harmony, who were going to do away with attitudes of the past, acted. This is what one of their best friends, a great follower of John, had to say:
Our claim for increased revenues from this source received short shrift at the hands of the Minister of Finance. He maintained that his own budgetary situation would not permit any further "concessions" to the provinces. This was a position we could not in all logic accept.
Maybe they could not accept it in logic, but they could not pry anything out of the Minister of Finance either. I continue:
This stand suggests that a province's entitlement-
I hope some of those hon. members who are such great exponents of provincial autonomy are listening to this.
This stand suggests that a province's entitlement to a share of taxation revenue is based on whether or not Canada feels she can afford it.
That is what Mr. Roblin is saying about a Tory government. I continue:
But the provinces are not mere residual partners in the Canadian confederation.
This is a Tory premier talking about a Tory Minister of Finance in Ottawa. I continue:
We cannot accept the implication that we must wait for some unstated level of dominion revenue before we receive recognition of our just rights.
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
Two years, only two years, and this is what we get.
To do so would be contrary to the whole principle and spirit of confederation.
This is the Tory premier saying that what the Minister of Finance is doing is contrary to the whole spirit and principle of confederation.
I venture to suggest it would be contrary to the
interests of Canada itself.
Then he went on:
We were unable to persuade the Minister of Finance to recommend to his colleagues any further changes in the level of tax-sharing. We have not given up hope-
Mr. Roblin can go on hoping but I do not think his hopes are worth much.
-for an improvement in 1961-62, but it likely will be 1962-63 before we can expect to secure a more realistic share of the taxation pool.
That is as good a friend as the government has left today after two years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Purely a coincidence.

-I was just about to refer to one or two other observations made by Mr. Roblin in his budget speech. In case this has not been drawn to the attention of the Minister of Finance, I feel that it should be drawn to his attention. Mr. Roblin said:
One of the advances made in the 1955 and 1956 negotiations-
That was when what we were doing was incomprehensible and inadequate, as the Minister of Finance said, but the premier of Manitoba does not seem to think so.
-was the recognition of the principles of equalization and stabilization.
This is very important, because for at least six of the provinces this is the differ-erence between life and death. The principles of equalization and stabilization are the difference between having autonomy and not having autonomy. Mr. Roblin went on to say:
It is true that there was a substantial element of fiscal need contained within the rental payments of the 1947 and 1952 tax agreements-
This is a great tribute from a Tory premier to the Liberal government and to what Mr. Harris and Mr. St. Laurent did in 1956.
-but it was not until the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act of 1956 that these two principles received open statutory acceptance.
Here is the premier of Manitoba saying that the system we have now is the system that Manitoba needs. It is the system, of course, that every one of the six provinces that could not possibly finance within their own limits has to have if they are to have any real autonomy, and I can tell you that the $60 million Quebec is getting by way of an equalization payment is pretty necessary to Quebec too. The provincial treasurer then went on to commend the government, as I have commended it every time I have mentioned the subject, for establishing the Atlantic provinces grants. I say that that is the one and only useful thing the government has done since it has been in office. Here is what Mr. Roblin said about it:
Unfortunately, Canada was not prepared to accept the logic of its own conclusions.
By "Canada" he means the Tory government.
The payments were limited to the four eastern provinces and were not extended to any other that might, under like conditions, be able to qualify
Dominion-Provincial Relations under the formula. We may, however, reasonably hope that the principle, having once been accepted, will in the next fiscal arrangement be carried to its logical and equitable conclusion.
So say I, and so says the leader of the opposition in Nova Scotia, Mr. Hicks, who promptly made this suggestion at the very time these Atlantic grants were started, and in equity it is the only fair way to do it. Mr. Roblin goes on:
The continued acceptance and extension of the .ioint principles of equalization and stabilization are basic principles on which any Manitoba case must be founded.
I repeat, "The continued acceptance and extension of the joint principles of equalization and stabilization". I remind you, sir, that these principles of equalization and stabilization were fought by the Tory party when it was in opposition. They were going to substitute a new system of allocation of tax fields. Any system of allocation of tax fields would be absolutely ruinous to six provinces in this country, and Mr. Roblin has made it very clear that he recognizes that fact. He says:
The continued acceptance and extension of the joint principles of equalization and stabilization are basic principles on which any Manitoba case must be founded. These are not concessons to this province, either on the part of Canada or any other province. They are essential factors in maintaining the rightful status of the provinces in the Canadian economy. These principles remain paramount. It will be our objective to see that they are applied in a formula more effective than that existing at the present time.
If a more effective formula can be found no one on this side of the house will oppose it, but until it is found we certainly stand by the formula that Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris introduced, that the hon. member for Bellechasse gave a blessing to, and that the Tory premier of Manitoba has said is essential to the preservation of provincial autonomy and equality among the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few brief remarks. First I wish to thank the Minister of Finance for settling a problem that has been existing for too long, that of giving all provinces a share in the aid to universities. I should also like to thank the hon. member for Bellechasse for the remarks he made about the help that the province of Quebec gives to French colleges outside of that province. It is probably doubtful whether such help is within the constitution. Hon. members all know that the provisions contained in section 93 and 133 of the British North America Act, which relate to separate schools and the French language, are equivalent to sections 22 and 23 of the Manitoba Act which was passed in 1870 and which granted the same privileges with respect to schools and language as have been granted to the minority in the province of Quebec.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I am happy to say that the province of Quebec has treated the English Protestant minority very well and I hope that the province of Quebec will always do so. But although in Manitoba we have the same constitutional rights as the province of Quebec, as all hon. members know, we have lost all our rights. We have left no vestige of the rights that were granted by our own provincial constitution.
Recently a royal commission was formed to study educational problems in Manitoba. The five members brought in a unanimous report advising the provincial government to grant 80 per cent of the amount paid to public schools for the support of separate and private schools. However, since that time the Winnipeg Free Press, that great Liberal paper which supports freedom for the South Africans and freedom all over the world, is exhibiting intolerance at home by advocating that the people who support separate schools pay double taxes. I have faith in the tolerance of my fellow English and Protestant citizens in the province of Manitoba. There are always bigots like the Winnipeg Free Press fanning the flames of intolerance.
I should like also to challenge a few of the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur when he attacked the hon. member for Bellechasse for advocating the right of the province of Quebec to help maintain French culture outside of the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Port Arthur said, are you in favour of a continuation of strife? I do not believe that merely because the French speaking Canadians outside Quebec fight for the maintenance of their culture they are continuing strife. It is just a struggle to keep their own culture.
If one reads the speeches of D'Arcy McGee, Brown, Macdonald, Cartier or even Mr. Rose, who represented Montreal Centre you will find that confederation was a partnership between the French and English races in Canada. Unless both cultures are treated equally, we will never have perfect unity in Canada. I do not believe we should try to argue on the basis of the British North America Act or even to stand on the Manitoba act of 1870, but we should lay more stress on the good will of Canadians generally. Unless we treat one another as equals, there will never be harmony, and it is only through harmony that Canadian unity can exist.

speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I began some remarks, a few minutes before the house was called to the hon. Senate. I shall try to complete what I wanted to say before the time set aside for the discussion of private bills.
I mentioned yesterday that we have now a trans-Canada highway which allows all Canadian citizens and indeed many transportation companies to travel entirely on Canadian soil.
I realize, following the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) that conditions west of Port Arthur, towards Winnipeg, do not seem too favourable. It nevertheless remains that there is now a trans-Canada highway. And, as I said yesterday, I was surprised to find that the hon. minister did not, even this year, choose to consider the inclusion in his resolution of a second trans-Canada highway, which could easily exist; not that I am opposed to the present route which goes through the south eastern and northern parts of Ontario, but I believe it would interest the minister to know conditions as they are now.
Indeed, we should admit that from a national defence point of view, we should have the necessary roads, in case of an attack.
Perhaps we do not realize that it might be easy to supply with an alternate route the people of northern Ontario and those of the northwest section of the province of Quebec. I said yesterday that there is now a practicable road, and paved for the most part between Longlac and North Bay, through Hearst, Kapuskasing and Cochrane. Now we would have to open a new road linking the northeastern part of the province of Ontario to the northwestern portion of the province of Quebec. That will leave only a 52-mile stretch of road to build, which after all does not mean an extraordinary expenditure, since the road from Cochrane to Hearst, which I mentioned a moment ago, is almost paved.
It seems to me that such a road would be advantageous because it would give us direct access to the west or allow us to reach cities


like Montreal and Quebec, so that we could travel on the road going through the Lau-rentian park. I say that that road would be necessary even for national defence purposes, especially if the government relies so much on the famous Bomarc installations- I do not intend to wander away from the resolution-because it just so happens that our region is, neither more nor less, under the umbrella where the famous Bomarc can cause the greatest damage. And there may be a time when the people of Kapuskasing, Hearst, Smooth Rock Falls, Cochrane and even of the Quebec part of the Abitibi may have to exacuate those twons as a result of what damage the famous Bomarc may cause there.
Therefore, I feel that the government should study that situation seriously. I remember that during the second world war, the Ontario provincial government, in order to contribute to the protection of the country as far as national defence was concerned, undertook to build a 163 mile stretch of road between Hearst and Longlac, which resulted in our having the existing trans-Canada highway.
It seems to me that the minister might have included in his resolution the building of a second direct road between the northern part of Ontario and the northwestern part of Abitibi.
In addition to being useful for national defence purposes, the building of such a road would supply jobs for the people of Abitibi and for the population of northeastern Ontario, because many lumber camps are operating in that area. At present, as we know, even the wood-workers return home by car every night so as not to remain overnight in the lumber camps.
This could also be a very interesting project for the tourist industry. I would therefore ask the minister to consider this matter because it is only a question of 52 miles. I must also point out, Mr. Chairman, that a survey was made in 1937-38 and that, but for the war of 1939, I am convinced this road would have been built by now.

On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, there are four children in this case, ages 15, 12, 9 and 6 respectively. As I have said before, we should consider the welfare of the children in these cases especially if the divorce is granted. The marriage took place in 1943 and there is a long history of marital discord resulting in desertion.
At page 12 of the evidence the divorce committee of the Senate thoroughly examined into the matter. 1 propose to refer to this evidence to illustrate the amount of weight given to the background of the marriage as compared to that given to the circumstances relating to adultery.
Mr. M. Joyal of Ottawa appeared as counsel for the petitioner. He examined into the background of the marriage and at page 12 the following evidence is recorded:
Q. You are not living with your husband at the moment?
A. No.
I point out that Mr. Joyal asked a leading question almost suggesting the answer. I continue:
Q. When did you separate from him? Or did you separate more than once from him?
A. Yes, about three or four times.
Obviously Mr. Joyal knew the answer before it was given. I continue:
Q. What were the grounds or reasons?
A. Promiscuity and alcoholism.
Q. Was this promiscuity and alcoholism the subject of some conversation between you and your husband?
A. Yes. it was.
Q. On one occasion, or on many occasions?
A. On many occasions.
Q. Did you ever resume cohabitation with him after he might have made certain promises?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. Were those promises kept?
A. No.
Q. Did he resume, so to speak, his habits of alcoholism and promiscuity?
A. Yes, he did.
Q. Forgetting about the alcoholism, which is a problem in itself, what about his promiscuous habits? Was it with one person?
A. Just about everybody.
Q. With any one person, was it over a short period of time or a more extended period of time?
A. Once, for a year and a half, and the last time about a year and a half.
By the Chairman (Senator Taylor, Westmorland):
Q. What do you mean by a year and a half?
A. Well-
Q. Was he keeping company with another woman for a year and a half?
A. Yes.

Private Bills-Divorce
Q. Do you know that to be a tact personally?
A. Yes. He took her out in public I know that, indeed. I know where she lived-the last one he lived with.
By Senator Barbour:
Q. Did they live together for a year and a half?
A. Oh yes.
By the Chairman (Senator Taylor, Westmorland) :
Q. He left you entirely and went to live with this woman?
A. Yes.

A. No. he did not come back after that.
The evidence indicates a series of desertions and reconciliations resulting in a final desertion. Mr. Joyal and the hon. senators were concerned about the question of desertion and what may be characterized as cruelty, involving alcoholism, extended promiscuity, the failure to keep promises and ultimate desertion. I shall return later to the subject of cruelty.
Some evidence was given concerning arrangements for the maintenance of the children. Mr. Joyal questioned the petitioner about this and the following exchange is recorded at page 13 of the evidence:
By Senator Barbour:
Q. Did he support you?

A. Yes.

A. Yes, it was.

A. Yes, and beating.

A. Yes.

A. Yes.

A. Yes.

A. Yes, I have been.
By the Chairman (Senator Taylor, Westmorland) :
Q. What was the amount?
A. $50 a week.
Q. For both yourself and the children?
A. Yes.
By Senator Barbour:
Q. That would be for the children, would it?
A. Well, yes.
By Mr. Joyal:

Q. Was that $50 a week for yourself and the children or for the children alone?
A. Well, when we had the separation it was for myself and the children.
I take it from the evidence, therefore, that $50 a week is provided for the wife and children. I think it is an excellent thing to conduct an examination into the question of maintenance in cases where there are children. It is apparent that the Senate pays not much attention. In fact, they feel they should not do this sort of thing, and ask questions about maintenance of children. I am quite sure, in their moral concept of these things they know full well we are liable to a degree if we are to be asked to pass a divorce bill. We are liable to the extent anyway of wondering about and concerning ourselves with the welfare, maintenance and upkeep of the children following the granting of the divorce
Even though some days ago the hon. member for Halifax raised, and quite properly so, the matter of jurisdiction because of the division of jurisdiction, and the question of this committee having the function of concerning itself with the maintenance of the children, and even though the chairman, at that time ruled that, because maintenance was not a matter upon which we could pass judgment, we should not concern ourselves with it, I do hope that the chairman of the committee at this time will be more lenient in this regard, certainly to the extent at least that the committee of the other place has been lenient in this regard in wanting to concern itself about the welfare of the children.
It is a commendable attitude for the members of the other place to take, and we would be well advised to follow their example. I do not say we should disregard the rules; I do not want to do that, but we should give expression to our moral thinking when it comes to the maintenance of the children.
When it comes to the actual grounds which are considered in granting a divorce we find that this case is similar to another one to which I had the opportunity to make reference the other day. One of the private eyes in this case again is Mr. Charles Char-ron, age 53, Montreal, Quebec who, I believe I indicated, has also been an investigator, whatever that is, in these cases. He has appeared as a witness in some 36 cases before the committee in the other place this year. If I am wrong in that figure I stand to be corrected. In his activities in those cases and in other years he is well aware of divorce proceedings; he is well aware of the points he is required to make to ensure that the proper-I put it that way generously -evidence is given to the committee of the

-and he came on the 5th of April at 12.35 in the morning.

We went to the door upstairs-it is a duplex. We knocked on the door several times before Mr.- came and opened the door. When he opened the door all he had on was a pair of grey pants with the upper part of his b.v.d.'s.
Perhaps he had a tie on.

It would be much more amusing if one could hear these interjections. I do not know whether he had a tie on or not; it is not given in evidence. From what we know of divorce evidence it could well be that he had a shirt and a tie underneath the top of his pyjamas to make it look well. The people who arrange divorce evidence

are not beyond that sort of thing. Let me return to the evidence given by Mr. Charron:
I asked, "Are you Mr.-?" He said yes. I showed him this photograph and he admitted that it was one taken of him.
This is 12.35 in the morning. The couple came in at a quarter after eleven, and 15 minutes later the gentleman is wearing the upper part of his b.v.d.'s. He is a complete stranger, but this investigator goes to the door, asks him his name, shows him a photograph and he says, "Yes, that is I". Is it reasonable to assume that one would expect this to take place? However, let me carry on with the evidence:
I went to the bedroom and asked the woman, who was in bed, her name.
Two strangers knock on the door at 12.35 in the morning; the gentleman wearing the upper part of his b.v.d.'s-with or without tie, it is not clear-and a pair of trousers, opens the door to two complete strangers and says, "Yes, this is my name." These two complete strangers walk into the house, duplex or apartment go into the bedroom and ask the woman there who was in bed, what her name was. No permission was asked. There was no difficulty; it was just like walking into Eaton's store to buy some clothing. They had complete freedom of the house. It was almost as if each of the parties involved in this, the two strangers, the investigators, the respondent and the corespondent knew precisely what was about to happen. It looks as if they were developing a stage presentation and had rehearsed this on a number of occasions. Let me return to the questions and answers:
And she said, "This is Mrs.-
She gave her surname, the name of the respondent. I continue:
Then I said, "What is your maiden name?" And she said-
She gave her maiden name. I continue:
The man asked what it was for-.
After these two strangers had knocked on the door at 12.35, after they had asked him his name and after they had shown the photograph he identified it as one of himself. After that they casually strolled into the living room or wherever it was, nonchalantly appeared in the bedroom, asked the woman in bed what her name was and then the respondent who was in his b.v.d.'s finally got the opportunity to ask what it was all about. Then he is told that divorce proceedings are involved and, to quote the evidence, "he started to get mad at us, so I told him to see a lawyer and we went out".

What Mr. Charron probably does is to mimeograph thousands of copies of his evidence. When he has to appear before a committee he just fills in the blanks on the mimeographed form with the names of the people involved and the times. As far as the evidence is concerned, it is almost identical, and it is stretching the imagination quite a bit to ask us to think that no arrangement existed between these people, that Mr. Charron did not know what he was going to find and that the couple in the apartment did not know that he was going to be there at a particular time.
We could assume that it might have happened if this were an isolated case and if the evidence in this case were unique but, as I say, it is not unique. It is stereotyped in form as if the investigator had memorized it and uses it each time he appears as a witness before the divorce committee. From that I think one must come to the conclusion that arrangements were made to obtain this evidence and that the evidence of Mr. Charron was given in such a way as only to satisfy the tests that might reasonably lead one to believe that adultery had taken place or might take place. That is the extent of the evidence here. The evidence with respect to adultery can be stretched, and if one looked at the evidence given here with both eyes closed and read it he could come to the conclusion-
That is a logical remark from a logical corner of the house.

It is a good Irish type of remark that the hon. member for Halifax will appreciate very much because so far as the evidence in this case is concerned, and I emphasize this, you do not need to read it to know that it is falsified.
Do you never believe anyone who speaks under oath in a court or do you believe just what you want to believe?
Perhaps the hon. member for Halifax would like to participate in the debate.
I will.

If he wants to ask questions I suggest that he do so in the normal manner by rising in his place instead of sitting in his seat and yapping about C.C.F. hypocrisy, knowing full well that at the time he did it he was not going to be called to order for making such slanderous charges.

I rise on a point of order. Surely it is not in order in this debate to refer to remarks made in previous debates. I realize that the hon. member is straying far and wide, but surely that is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It is also a rule in this committee for one person to have the floor at a time. The hon. member for Skeena.

I am pleased that the hon. member for Halifax did get around to participating in the correct manner and I hope he will continue to do so as we deal with other cases. As I have said, I think the evidence with respect to adultery in respect to this particular case was arranged beforehand and was designed to meet the minimum tests established with respect to adultery. Because of the extensive questioning by members of the other place and also by Mr. Joyal, counsel for the petitioner, with respect to desertion, alcoholism, cruelty and extended promiscuity, I believe that is the basis upon which this divorce was granted by the Senate and that the adultery was only an incidental factor. I submit this was the decent and correct thing to do. I am told by people who have had far more experience than I have with regard to the granting of divorces by parliament that it is only by practice that the test of adultery has been established and that parliament can grant a divorce upon any ground or no ground at all. Whether or not that is correct I do not know. As I say, my information comes from a source that I consider to be quite reliable and I take their word for it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: One was granted the other day for desertion.
The hon. member for Timis-kaming comments that the Senate granted a divorce the other day on the basis of desertion.
Untrue.

I assume they have done the same thing in this case. I assume that the greatest amount of weight has been given to the questions of desertion and cruelty and that the reference to adultery is only there to leave the impression that the unofficial rules followed in these cases have been met. I certainly think that the divorce should be granted.
I could make some reference to the manner in which Mr. Joyal asked questions, which was more a case of insisting upon a certain type of answer than asking questions. It might be well to read some of them. As found on page 14, Mr. Joyal is examining the petitioner. There have been some questions by members of the Senate about other matters and Mr. Joyal comes to the question of arrangements between the petitioner and the respondent. He does not say, as one would normally expect, "Have you made any arrangements," He says:
Q. You made no arrangements with your husband whereby he could provide this evidence so that this action could be taken?

He practically puts the answer in the woman's mouth. She said, "Oh, no". Again, there is this direct statement:
Q. There has been no connivance? You have not got together and put through a little deal with Miss ... so that your husband would be caught with her?
A. I would not speak to her.
You will notice that she did not answer the question directly. However, we can assume from that that the answer is no because the lawyer said it was no. Again, we have this extensive question and a very short answer:
Q. I take it, because of these repeated separations and reconciliations, you feel that the marriage is on the rocks now, and you have not forgiven your husband in the sense of being prepared to resume cohabitation with him?
If anyone could answer "yes" to that type of question it would be a strange thing indeed. However, the answer was "Oh, no". Then there is this question:
Q. Whatever difficulties you have, do you think they will be increased should this divorce be granted to you?
The answer is obvious. You do not have to read it. The answer is "No". Then she goes further and says:
I could not have any increase in my difficulties.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, on the basis of cruelty, promiscuity on a number of occasions-
The Depuiy Chairman: I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a particularly mischievous type of intervention in the debate on this particular case and I intend to deal with several points made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. Ordinarily, I would content myself, but I am afraid I have reached a point where I cannot sit here in the House of Commons among certain other gentlemen and hear hon. members from one particular corner assassinate the characters of people who are not here and able to defend themselves. The first point,-
Let them get their divorces somewhere else.

-and one that has gained some currency throughout this country because of remarks made on previous occasions and repeated this afternoon is that divorces are being granted on grounds other than adultery. This is just not so. If that impression got abroad it would lead people who went to provincial courts for justice into thinking that some special favours were being dispensed in parliament that were not given elsewhere. I think that is mischievous and I so brand it.
Private Bills-Divorce
The hon. member has also made it appear, by reading carefully selected portions of the evidence, as if the alleged adultery between the respondent husband and his lady friend were staged. If the hon. member had wanted to fairly present all the evidence on that matter he would have found in the evidence of the wife, at the top of page 14, that actually the husband and this woman had been living together for quite a period of time. It is this sort of remark, this loose allegation, that I am afraid I can no longer take. If my hon. friend is going through this stack of cases one by one and making such remarks, then somebody is going to defend the people who cannot defend themselves here and I am afraid it is going to be a long, hard session.

I am afraid I cannot very well allow these comments to go by without straightening out the record and, at the same time, straightening out the hon. member for Halifax. If he had been listening carefully, as I assume he did, he would have heard what I said about the evidence I read and he would have had no occasion to make the rather unfair and unkind remarks he made a moment ago. If he was not listening when I made my initial remarks, then I forgive him and I shall attempt to repeat what I said with respect to this particular case.
The hon. member said that I carefully selected sections from the evidence, and carefully left out others, in order to leave the impression that this evidence was staged. He said that if I had read a certain piece of evidence it would have shown that this couple had been living together for some time. I have my notes here and I will read again what I read before. It is at the bottom of page 12. There is another place in the evidence in which these facts are more clearly stated, but Mr. Joyal is questioning the witness about the husband living with other people. I start reading in the middle of one question:
Was it with one person?
A. Just about everybody.
Q. With any one person, was it over a short period of time or a more extended period of time?
A. Once, for a year and a half, and the last time about a year and a half.
Q. What do you mean by a year and a half?
A. Well-
Q. Was he keeping company with another woman for a year and a half?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you know that to be a fact personally?
A. Yes. He took her out in public. I know that, indeed. I knew where she lived-the last one he lived with.
Q. Did they live together for a year and a half?
A. Oh, yes.

Private Bills-Divorce
Q. He left you entirely and went to live with this woman?
A. Yes.
Q. And he came back again to you?
A. No, he did not come back after that.
It is true that later on, on page 14, this point is more clearly drawn to the attention of the committee. This is probably the quotation to which the hon. member for Halifax was referring. I read:
Q. Was this the same woman he lived with for a year and a half?
A. Yes, but he only lived with her after I had met her.
The evidence which I read initially did bring out the fact that there was a person with whom he lived for a year and a half. I believe that evidence of that nature itself, when it is not contested or denied, is just as valid evidence to show that adultery took place as the evidence is of going through all these formalities of people knocking on doors after 12.30, walking into the bedroom, asking for names, showing photographs, and so on; all for the purpose of meeting certain tests that have been established. I submit that this evidence given on page 13 to the effect that he was going with some woman for a year and a half, and that he lived with her, is a greater indication that adultery could have taken place than the circumstances related on page 15 by Mr. Charron in which he happens to walk casually into this place and find someone in his b.v.d.'s and a pair of grey pants in the bedroom. There is far more chance that adultery took place during the course of this friendship over a year and a half than there would be that it took place at the moment Mr. Charron entered this place.
The hon. member for Halifax made mention of the fact that these two people lived together for a year and a half. I think there is a greater likelihood that adultery might have taken place in that year and a half rather than in the few short minutes Mr. Charron was wandering around in that particular apartment. The hon. member for Halifax also made some comments to the effect that some of us, I presume in the C.C.F., were engaged in a game of character assassination with respect to people who were not here to defend themselves. I know the hon. member wants to be fair in this matter, and in all other matters, and I admit that in dealing with the earlier cases and reading from the evidence, if the name of the respondent was given I read the name of the respondent; if the name of the corespondent was given I read that name and I also read the address because those names and addresses appeared in the evidence. It was only when the hon. member

for Halifax rose to ask me a question during a previous case and, instead of reading the name of the individual left it blank, that I realized I had been in error in the other cases when I made reference to the names of the individuals. I spoke to the hon. member for Halifax about this afterwards and thanked him for drawing this to my attention in an indirect way. Since that time, I have made no references to the names of the petitioners, the respondents, the corespondents or their addresses. The only names I have mentioned have been those of the lawyers and investigators.
Would the hon. member permit a question. He has referred to a local lawyer in connection with this case. Is he suggesting the lawyer acted improperly in this particular case?
I do not know how the hon. member could come to that strange conclusion.

The hon. member referred to the evidence during the early part of the discussion and made some remarks about the lawyer's questioning of the witness. There was a suggestion that they had come to some agreement prior to giving testimony.

My friend who is asking this question is a lawyer. I imagine that when he represents someone he goes over the evidence with him, goes over the story, and attempts to get it straight in his mind; that is one thing. The second thing is that it is my understanding a lawyer is in a profession, and one of his functions is to represent people. He is certainly not involved. He is not a respondent or a corespondent. If, for argument's sake, Joyal was mentioned as respondent or corespondent or petioner in any one of these cases, I would not mention his name as that. But I do not see that there is much wrong in making reference to the name of the particular lawyer who is involved in the case because this is his function as a public servant, as I understand it, or as a servant of his client and the same thing applies as well in the case of the private investigators. They have a particular duty to perform. The position is just the same as when reference is made to the name of Senator Taylor who is chairman of the committee. This implies nothing whatsoever with regard to Senator Taylor. He is a member of the Senate. He is chairman of the committee and he asks certain questions. I do not see that there is anything wrong in that procedure.
I conclude that the hon. member is not suggesting that there was any improper conduct on the part of the lawyer.
I do not know whether there was or not.
Answer the question.

I made no such suggestion.
I do not know how my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard could have come to that conclusion.
It is very hard to follow the hon. member.

I did say-and I will say it again-that Mr. Joyal is quite adept at asking questions in such a way that he gets a particular answer. I assume that this is one of the things a lawyer is trained to do.
I am not a lawyer, and I do not know what the situation is but I assume that one of the functions of a lawyer, if he is retained by a client, is to protect and to advance the interest of that client in court or in some other place if that is where he is acting on the client's behalf.
If by his line of questioning he desires to get certain information out, then this is his function, is it not? I suggest that he is quite good at that sort of thing. Perhaps he should have a "Q.C." after his name-as have so many other lawyers in Ontario-for his skill and ability in making sure that the interests of his client,-in this case the petitioner, are presented to the fullest extent, that her case is advanced and that the evidence given is in her favour. If evidence is given which is not in her favour, he will on cross-examination, if it is a contested case, do his best so to confound other persons giving evidence that it will be to the advantage of his particular client. I do not see anything wrong in that procedure. Maybe I have a misunderstanding of one of the functions of members of the legal profession. However,
I would assume that this is one of them, namely that of advancing the interests of their clients.
I say only that Mr. Joyal is very skilful and adept at this procedure and when he wants the answer no, he phrases the question in such a way that he gets the answer no. Whether he sat down with the petitioner in this case beforehand, went over the evidence and discussed the questions which might be asked of her by him or by the senators, I do not know. Quite frankly, I may say that I do not know whether or not this is a common practice followed by lawyers with clients. Perhaps my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard could take the opportunity of advising us on the matter out of his wealth of legal knowledge and ability, and the cases with which he has dealt.
