speechtext:
I have an important announcement relating to the applications for the export of gas and for the construction of gas pipe lines which have been considered by the national energy board.
Recognizing the economic importance of energy to the future growth and development of our country and realizing that a national energy policy is fundamental to our national development program, one of the first decisions of this government was to establish a national energy board.
The board has been set up to assure the people of Canada that the best possible use is made of the energy resources of this country. It is charged, among other things, with the responsibility, subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, of regulating the construction and operation of oil and gas pipe lines, the tolls charged for transmission by such pipe lines, and the export and import of gas in such a manner that the public interest is protected. The board is also charged with the responsibility of safeguarding Canada's interest in regard to the methods of financing and the participation of Canadians in the pipe lines that transmit energy under the jurisdiction of parliament.
I now wish to table two copies of the important report of the national energy board on application for licences to export natural

Tabling of Energy Board Report gas and build certain pipe lines for the purpose, and to announce the decisions of the government in regard to the approvals required under the law.
After a detailed review of the applications and the circumstances affecting each of them, based upon the lengthy public hearings it held, the board states that it is prepared to issue, subject to approval of the government as required by law, and upon certain defined conditions, the following export licences:
(a)	a licence to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to export a maximum of 204 million cubic feet of gas per day near Emerson, Manitoba;
(b)	a further licence to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to export a maximum of 204 million cubic feet of gas per day, on an interruptible basis, near Niagara Falls, Ontario;
(c)	a licence to Alberta and Southern Gas Company Limited to export a maximum of 458,750,000 cubic feet of gas per day near Kingsgate, British Columbia;
(d)	a licence to Canadian-Montana Pipe Line Company to export a maximum of 36 million cubic feet of gas per day at a point on the boundary near Cardston, Alberta; and
(e)	a licence to Westcoast Transmission Company Limited to export a maximum of 152 million cubic feet of gas per day near Kingsgate, British Columbia.
The board has also stated that is it prepared to issue, subject to approval of the government and upon certain defined conditions, certificates of public convenience and necessity authorizing the construction of pipe lines as follows:
(a)	To Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited for the construction of a 30-inch pipe line from lie des Chenes in Manitoba to the international boundary near Emerson, Manitoba, a distance of approximately 51 miles;
(b)	To Alberta Natural Gas Company for the construction of a 36-inch pipe line from a point in southwestern Alberta to the international boundary near Kingsgate, British Columbia, a total distance of approximately 108 miles;
(c)	To Canadian-Montana Pipe Line Company for the construction of a 16-inch pipe line, approximately three miles in length, in southern Alberta near the international boundary near Cardston, Alberta.
The board estimates that the annual revenue of the exports of gas covered by these licences would amount in all by 1963 to about $75 million. In addition, the development of the fields and the construction of the pipe lines, gathering lines and processing facilities would

involve investments over the next few years amounting to several hundred millions of dollars.
The board considered, but did not approve, an application from Niagara Gas Transmission Limited for a licence to export gas near Cornwall, Ontario, and authority to build a short pipe line for the purpose. The board was not satisfied that the price to be charged by the applicant for the gas proposed to be exported was just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
In its report upon these applications for licences the board states its finding that, having regard to established reserves and to the trends in the discovery of gas, there is now sufficient gas to meet the reasonably foreseeable requirements for use in Canada and to permit exports on the scale proposed. The board also found that the terms on which the exports will be made under the licences proposed are fair and reasonable.
The government has fully considered this major report of the board and has concluded that the findings and decisions of the board assure the protection of the public interest of Canada and Canadians.
The government has given special attention to the export licence proposed for the Westcoast Transmission company, having in mind the observations made in the first report of the royal commission on energy in 1958, on the existing Westcoast contract for exports at Sumas.
The government has considered the views of the board concerning the increased utilization of the present pipe line operated by Westcoast and the desirability of developing more reserves of gas in northern British Columbia.
When applications are made for the issue of future licences for the export of gas to Pacific coast areas of the United States, a primary consideration the government will have in mind is whether the action proposed will have the effect of increasing the use of the existing Westcoast pipe line and further promoting the development and use of exportable gas reserves in British Columbia. In carrying out such a policy it is expected that as the demand for gas increases in the Pacific areas of the United States, the prices to be obtained from export sales of British Columbia gas will in due course increase substantially, thereby effectively offsetting the unduly low price in the existing export contract entered into in December 1954.
Accordingly the government has decided that it will authorize the issue of such licences and certificates as have been approved by the board and on the terms set

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house and the country at large will welcome this announcement. There has been a long delay in dealing with these matters because of the time which elapsed before the energy board was set up and the policy in that regard announced. That factor, together with the delay after the energy board was authorized in appointing the board itself, and also the time consumed by the necessary hearings, does make up quite a lapse of time, and I am very sure that now the announcement has been made it will be most welcome to the country at large.
The rather interesting thing here is that the government fortunately has announced the granting of the necessary licences to the company which in earlier days it so vehemently opposed and attacked in this house, and I think it has very effectively vindicated the stand taken by the former government in this regard. I think this is a very good thing for the country at large, as well as for the industry.
The payments which will arise out of this export are also welcome at this time because of the effect they will have on our balance of payments with the United States. That is a very good and important feature, and the licences will provide as well a lift to the internal economy of Canada arising directly out of the necessary development work.
I take it from the minister's announcement that the government has in fact, either wholly or very substantially accepted the findings of the national energy board. It is a happy circumstance to see that that has happened because there was an interesting point which arose so far as the export licences themselves were concerned in that the energy board act gives to the national energy board under section 82 a right to issue the licences. In section 85 it gives the governor in council certain very limited rights to make regulations. Under those limited rights to make regulations the governor in council has seen fit to claim the right to approve the granting of export licences by the board. I doubt very much if the governor in council has that right to take something that parliament did not give it. But in this particular case, as I understand the announcement, the question does not arise because the government is in fact approving the granting of the licences by the board as the board has recommended.
Tabling of Energy Board Report If 1 am right on that point, the question does not arise and I think that is a fortunate circumstance. The point can perhaps be more appropriately and aptly developed on some other occasion.
I think the minister is quite correct in speaking about the lift, if I may use that term, that these licences will give to the economy of Canada at this time when it is needed. It will be a very good thing for the country and the announcement is timely for the reason that the economy, in my view at least, needs this added lift at this time. The minister also gave some indication as to the commodity value of the export in 1963, and that is particularly welcome because it will go a considerable way to help to replace the loss of the uranium export in that year.
It is very difficult to appreciate fully every implication of the remarks contained in the minister's statement, and perhaps there are other parts of his statement on which it would be better to reserve comment. But I think it is appropriate that I should indicate that, as far as we are concerned, we welcome the making of this announcement today.

Mr. Speaker, speaking for this group in general terms in view of the lack of time to consider the announcement carefully and fully I must say I am sure all hon. members are pleased the minister made the announcement because of the importance of this matter to the Canadian economy.
Without doubt this decision is the result of study of the first major problem that is being given consideration by the energy board. I think it is quite proper to say that all hon. members have confidence in the personnel of the board.
It is obvious from the statement as I heard it that in this instance the government takes final responsibility for the decision. I listened as carefully as possible to mention of the export gas from certain points in Canada with many of which I am not familiar although I am acquainted with Crowsnest and Kingsgate. In view of the representations made by citizens, municipalities and various organizations in places from which gas is to be exported I take it that the interests of potential Canadian consumers with respect to service and price are well protected by this decision and that there is protection with respect to reserves.
We are all human and I suppose it is fair to say that only time and experience will

Business of the House
prove the wisdom of this decision. In the meantime, on behalf of this group I want to say we trust the announcement will mean the decision will result in a major contribution to the economy and consequently to the benefit of the Canadian people.
